Context: what Orthodox theology is and w.back: Greek: **speaking about God** (*Theos*, God; *logos*, word). In the Fathers: knowing God and speaking truly of Him, above all of the Trinity.

Context: what Orthodox theology is and w.front: How does the Orthodox Church know what she believes?
Context: what Orthodox theology is and w.back: **God reveals Himself; the Holy Spirit keeps the Church in the truth; the Church hands it on as one living Tradition**, witnessed by Scripture, councils, Fathers, services, icons, saints and canons.

The theologian is one who prays: theolog.front: Evagrius of Pontus on the theologian
The theologian is one who prays: theolog.back: Desert monk (about **345–399**). In *On Prayer* (paraphrased): **if you are a theologian you will pray truly, and if you pray truly you are a theologian.**
**St John the Evangelist**, **St Gregory of Nazianzus** and **St Symeon the New Theologian**.

The theologian is one who prays: theolog.front: Why is theology tied to prayer in Orthodox teaching?
The theologian is one who prays: theolog.back: Because theology is **knowledge of God as a person**, which comes from meeting Him. Study without prayer becomes talk; doctrine guards the field where prayer grows.

Purity of heart: why Gregory says not ev.front: St Gregory the Theologian and the Theological Orations
Purity of heart: why Gregory says not ev.back: Gregory of Nazianzus (about **329–390**). Preached the five **Theological Orations** in Constantinople in **380**. Feast **25 January**; one of the Three Hierarchs (30 January).

Purity of heart: why Gregory says not ev.front: Why does Gregory say not everyone may theologise? (Oration 27)
Purity of heart: why Gregory says not ev.back: Because knowledge of God needs a **purified soul and an undistracted mind**: "For the impure to touch the pure is... not safe." He was answering those who debated God as entertainment.
The three stages of the path to God: **purification** (κάθαρσις), **illumination** (φωτισμός), **deification** (θέωσις).

Revelation: how God makes himself known.back: **Revelation**, "uncovering": God making Himself known, which created minds cannot reach by their own power.

Revelation: how God makes himself known.front: What does the Church teach about the completeness of revelation?
Revelation: how God makes himself known.back: **In Christ revelation is complete**; nothing new about God is added after the apostles. What grows is the Church's understanding and expression of it.
Visions given to saints **confirm and illuminate** the faith but never add to it; a vision contradicting the faith is judged false.

Holy Tradition: what is handed down.back: **Tradition**, "handing down": the faith received from Christ and the apostles and passed on in the Church. 2 Thessalonians 2:15: "whether by word, or our epistle".
**Holy Tradition** is the faith itself and does not change; **local customs** grow around it and may change.
Vladimir Lossky (**1903–1958**): Tradition is **the life of the Holy Spirit in the Church**.

Scripture within Tradition.front: Does the Orthodox Church hold Scripture and Tradition as two sources?
Scripture within Tradition.back: **No: one Tradition with Scripture at its heart.** The Scriptures were written, gathered and read within the Church.
"**God-breathed**" (2 Timothy 3:16): Scripture is inspired, the Spirit speaking through human writers in their own words.
St Paul's title for **the Church** (1 Timothy 3:15).

St Basil on the written and unwritten tr.front: St Basil the Great, author of On the Holy Spirit
St Basil on the written and unwritten tr.back: Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia (about **330–379**); wrote *On the Holy Spirit* (about **375**). Feast **1 January**.

St Basil on the written and unwritten tr.front: What does Basil teach in On the Holy Spirit 27?
St Basil on the written and unwritten tr.back: Some of the Church's teaching is **written**, some **received by unwritten apostolic tradition**, and "both... have the same force".
The **sign of the cross**, **praying east**, the words of the **epiclesis**, blessing **baptismal water and oil**, **triple immersion**, the **renunciation of Satan**.

Faith and reason: theology and philosoph.front: What can reason do in Orthodox theology, and what can it not?
Faith and reason: theology and philosoph.back: It can **define terms, expose errors and show God exists** from creation. It **cannot comprehend God's essence** or discover the Trinity.

Faith and reason: theology and philosoph.front: Why did the Fathers borrow philosophical terms?
Faith and reason: theology and philosoph.back: To speak precisely of the Trinity and Christ; they took words like *ousia* and *hypostasis* and **gave them new meaning**, refusing to let philosophy dictate what God can be.

The seven ecumenical councils as witness.back: The apostles' council on Gentile converts; its letter begins "**it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us**" (Acts 15:28): the model of every council.
**No.** A council states what the Church has always believed, **in words that shut out a particular error**.

The seven ecumenical councils as witness.front: An eighth and ninth ecumenical council?
The seven ecumenical councils as witness.back: Some Orthodox count **Constantinople 879–880** and the **hesychast councils 1341–1351** as ecumenical; others say none since 787 has been formally so recognised. Both accept their teaching.

Reception: how a council is known to be.back: The Council of **Ephesus 449**, which upheld Eutyches by force; Pope Leo called it a *latrocinium*; overturned at **Chalcedon (451)**.

Reception: how a council is known to be.front: Council of Hieria (754): a rejected council
Reception: how a council is known to be.back: Iconoclast council of over 300 bishops that **called itself ecumenical**; rejected by **Nicaea II (787)**.

Reception: how a council is known to be.front: St Mark of Ephesus and the union of Florence
Reception: how a council is known to be.back: The one Greek bishop who **refused to sign the union of Florence (1439)**; the union was formally rejected in Constantinople in **1484**.

Reception: how a council is known to be.front: What makes a council truly ecumenical?
Reception: how a council is known to be.back: Not numbers or summons alone but **faithfulness to the Tradition, recognised by the whole Church in the Spirit** (reception).

Who counts as a Father of the Church.front: Four marks of a Father of the Church
Who counts as a Father of the Church.back: **Orthodox teaching**, **holiness of life**, **the Church's recognition**, and (loosely) **antiquity**.

Who counts as a Father of the Church.front: Has the age of the Fathers closed, in Orthodox teaching?
Who counts as a Father of the Church.back: **No.** The same Spirit raises up Fathers still: Symeon the New Theologian, Gregory Palamas and Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain are read as Fathers.
Sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa (about **327–379**), whom Gregory called "**the Teacher**".

The consensus of the Fathers.back: "**The agreement of the Fathers**": where the Fathers in different times and places teach the same as the faith of the Church, a sure witness to Tradition.
Fr Georges Florovsky's (**1893–1979**) call to think with **the mind of the Fathers**, not only quote them.

The consensus of the Fathers.front: Can a single Father outweigh the consensus?
The consensus of the Fathers.back: **No.** A Father can err on a point; authority lies in **what the Fathers hold in common**.

Reading: St Vincent of Lérins on what ha.back: Monk of Lérins off southern Gaul (died about **445**); wrote the *Commonitorium* in **434**. Commemorated **24 May**.

Reading: St Vincent of Lérins on what ha.front: The Vincentian canon: everywhere, always, by all
Reading: St Vincent of Lérins on what ha.back: "**That faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all**" (*ubique, semper, ab omnibus*).

Reading: St Vincent of Lérins on what ha.front: Vincent's three tests of the true faith
Reading: St Vincent of Lérins on what ha.back: **Universality** (the whole Church), **antiquity** (the holy fathers), **consent** (the agreement of all or almost all teachers within antiquity).

Growth without change: St Vincent on dev.front: What progress does Vincent allow in doctrine? (Commonitorium 23)
Growth without change: St Vincent on dev.back: **Real progress, not alteration**: growth "in the same doctrine, in the same sense, and in the same meaning", like a child growing into a man.

Growth without change: St Vincent on dev.front: How has the Church's expression of the faith grown?
Growth without change: St Vincent on dev.back: By **new words for old truth** (*homoousios*, *Theotokos*), **clearer distinctions**, and **answers to new errors**: never by new content.

The services as theology: the rule of pr.front: Lex orandi, lex credendi: Prosper's principle
The services as theology: the rule of pr.back: Latin tag from **Prosper of Aquitaine** (5th century): **the rule of prayer sets the rule of belief**.
The **rule book of the services**: how to combine the Horologion, Octoechos, Menaion, Triodion and Pentecostarion each day.

The services as theology: the rule of pr.front: Octoechos: the book of eight tones
The services as theology: the rule of pr.back: The book of hymns in **eight tones** (ἦχος), sung in an eight-week cycle.

Icons and the lives of the saints as wit.front: Sunday of Orthodoxy and the restoration of icons
Icons and the lives of the saints as wit.back: **First Sunday of Great Lent**, recalling the restoration of icons in **843**.

Icons and the lives of the saints as wit.front: Why are icons possible, according to Nicaea II (787)?
Icons and the lives of the saints as wit.back: **Because God the Word became man and was seen**, He can be depicted; honour to the icon passes to the person shown.

Icons and the lives of the saints as wit.front: What does glorification of a saint mean?
Icons and the lives of the saints as wit.back: The Church **recognises** a saint God has already glorified, usually after popular veneration and a holy life, by synodal decision and new services.

The holy canons: akriveia and oikonomia.back: "**Exactness**": applying a canon strictly, as written.
"**Household management**": applying a canon with pastoral flexibility for a person's salvation. It bends the application, not the rule.
"**The Rudder**": the Greek collection of the canons with commentary by **St Nikodemos** and Agapios, published **1800**.

The holy canons: akriveia and oikonomia.front: Council in Trullo (692) and its canons
The holy canons: akriveia and oikonomia.back: The **Quinisext** council, issuing canons for the fifth and sixth councils; the East counts them as ecumenical.

Dogma, theologoumenon and private opinio.back: A **theological opinion** held by Fathers or many writers, compatible with dogma but **not defined**.

Dogma, theologoumenon and private opinio.front: How do you tell dogma from theologoumenon?
Dogma, theologoumenon and private opinio.back: Ask: **defined by a council? in the Creed or central services? taught by the Fathers with one voice?** If yes, dogma. If held by some Fathers but undefined, theologoumenon.
Teaching that the soul after death passes demonic "customs posts". **Held by some Orthodox** (Ignatius Brianchaninov, Seraphim Rose) as Church teaching; **others** (Lazar Puhalo) reject it as dogma.

Bishops and apostolic succession: Ignati.front: St Ignatius of Antioch and the bishop
Bishops and apostolic succession: Ignati.back: Bishop of Antioch, martyred in Rome (about **107–110**); wrote seven letters. First surviving use of "**the Catholic Church**" (Smyrnaeans 8).

Bishops and apostolic succession: Ignati.front: St Irenaeus of Lyons and apostolic succession
Bishops and apostolic succession: Ignati.back: About **130–202**; hearer of Polycarp; bishop of Lyons. Against the Gnostics, appealed to the **public succession of bishops** (*Against Heresies* 3.3).

Bishops and apostolic succession: Ignati.front: Is apostolic succession enough by itself?
Bishops and apostolic succession: Ignati.back: **No.** Succession of ordination and **faithfulness to the apostolic faith** go together; a bishop who abandons the faith loses the authority succession guards.
Russian: **conciliarity**, the Church's unity in freedom and love; used by **Alexei Khomiakov**.

The mind of the Church: phronema and the.back: "**Mind**" or outlook: the **mind of the Church**, formed by living in the Tradition.
Reply to Pius IX by the patriarchs of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem; held that **the guardian of the faith is the whole body of the Church, the people**.

The mind of the Church: phronema and the.front: Who are the bearers of the truth in the Orthodox Church?
The mind of the Church: phronema and the.back: **The whole people of God**, with the bishops as appointed teachers and witnesses, not owners, of the faith.

The Church in one map: the patriarchates.back: "**Being one's own head**": a local church that elects its own primate and governs itself, in one faith and communion with the others.

The Church in one map: the patriarchates.front: Diptychs: the order of the churches
The Church in one map: the patriarchates.back: The **list of primates** commemorated at the Liturgy, in order of honour. Constantinople and Moscow order it slightly differently.
Received **autocephaly from Moscow in 1970**; recognised by some churches, not by Constantinople.

Looking back: how the Church knows.front: The witnesses to Holy Tradition, in one line
Looking back: how the Church knows.back: **Scripture, unwritten tradition, councils, Fathers, services, icons and saints, canons, bishops, and the whole people**: one Tradition, one Spirit.

Looking back: how the Church knows.front: Why do the saints matter for knowing the faith?
Looking back: how the Church knows.back: Because theology is knowledge of God given to the purified: **the saints are the surest theologians**, and holiness confirms true teaching.

Context: the Creed and why the Church sa.back: The **Symbol of Faith**, the Creed: originally a token matching its other half, by which Orthodox Christians recognise one another's faith.
Drawn up at **Nicaea (325)**, completed at **Constantinople (381)**, confirmed at **Chalcedon (451)**; said unchanged ever since.

Context: the Creed and why the Church sa.front: Why does the Liturgy say "I believe" when the councils wrote "We believe"?
Context: the Creed and why the Church sa.back: The councils spoke as bishops together (*Pisteuomen*); in worship **each person confesses the faith of the whole Church as his own** (*Pisteuo*).

The Symbol of Faith: the text of Nicaea.front: What did Constantinople (381) add to the Creed of Nicaea?
The Symbol of Faith: the text of Nicaea.back: "Maker of **heaven and earth**", "before all worlds", the Virgin Mary and Pontius Pilate, "whose kingdom shall have no end", and **the whole article on the Holy Spirit**, the Church, baptism and the resurrection.
"**Giver of life**": the Creed's title for the Holy Spirit, who gives life as only God does.

Faith: what \"I believe\" means.back: **Faith, trust and faithfulness** at once. "I believe in" means "I put my trust in", not merely "I hold the opinion".

Faith: what \"I believe\" means.front: The two sides of faith in Orthodox teaching
Faith: what \"I believe\" means.back: **Trust** in God as a person and **assent** to what He has revealed; each without the other is not faith.
**Cooperation** of divine grace and human freedom: faith is God's gift, freely accepted.

Can God be known? Creation, conscience a.front: What can be known of God from creation, and what only by revelation?
Can God be known? Creation, conscience a.back: From creation: **that God exists, is powerful, wise and one** (Romans 1:20). Only by revelation: **the Trinity, the Incarnation, salvation**.

Can God be known? Creation, conscience a.front: Nous (νοῦς) and the knowledge of God
Can God be known? Creation, conscience a.back: The **spiritual intellect**, the eye of the soul, which perceives directly; distinct from step-by-step reasoning.

Can God be known? Creation, conscience a.front: Why, according to the Fathers, do many not know God?
Can God be known? Creation, conscience a.back: Not for lack of evidence but because **the passions darken the mind**; purification comes before vision.

One God: the faith of Israel and the Chu.back: "**Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD**" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Called by Christ the first commandment.

One God: the faith of Israel and the Chu.front: Does the Trinity contradict the oneness of God?
One God: the faith of Israel and the Chu.back: **No.** The Trinity is the one God of Israel revealed as Father, Son and Spirit; **the unity of God is the Trinity's unity**.

One God: the faith of Israel and the Chu.front: What does the Church teach against dualism?
One God: the faith of Israel and the Chu.back: There is **one God, wholly good**; evil is not a second principle but **a turning away from the good by free creatures**.

God the Father: the monarchy of the Fath.front: Monarchy of the Father as ground of unity
God the Father: the monarchy of the Fath.back: *Monarchia* (μοναρχία), "single source": **the Father is the one source and cause of the Son and the Spirit**, and the ground of God's unity.
"**Spring**" and "**cause**": the Fathers' words for the Father as source of the Son and Spirit.

God the Father: the monarchy of the Fath.front: Is God Father by nature or by adoption?
God the Father: the monarchy of the Fath.back: **By nature** of the eternal Son; **by adoption and grace** of those united to the Son in baptism.

Almighty: God the Pantokrator.back: "**The One who holds all things**" (*pan*, all; *krateo*, hold, rule): the Creed's "Almighty"; also the icon of Christ in the dome.

Almighty: God the Pantokrator.front: What does God's almightiness not mean?
Almighty: God the Pantokrator.back: Not that God does the **self-contradictory**, **wills evil**, or **overrides the freedom** He has given.

The divine Name: \"I am THE BEING\".back: "**The One who is**": the Septuagint's name of God at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14); written **Ο Ω Ν on the halo of Christ** in icons.

The divine Name: \"I am THE BEING\".front: Why is ho On written on Christ's halo?
The divine Name: \"I am THE BEING\".back: Because the Fathers taught that **the One who spoke to Moses was the eternal Word**, who later became man.
"**Lord**": the Septuagint's rendering of the divine Name YHWH; the New Testament's title for Jesus.

The Trinity revealed: Scripture, the The.front: Theophany (6 January) as revelation of the Trinity
The Trinity revealed: Scripture, the The.back: *Theophaneia*, "**appearance of God**": Christ's baptism in the Jordan, where **the Father speaks, the Son is baptised, the Spirit descends**.
Icon of **the three angels at Mamre** (Genesis 18) by **St Andrei Rublev**, early fifteenth century; held up as the model by the Stoglav council (1551).

The Trinity revealed: Scripture, the The.front: Why does the Orthodox Church call Pentecost "Trinity Sunday"?
The Trinity revealed: Scripture, the The.back: Because with the Spirit's coming **the whole Trinity is made known** and the Church is born.

Ousia and hypostasis: the words for one.back: **Person**: **who** God is. Three: Father, Son, Holy Spirit.

Ousia and hypostasis: the words for one.front: Where does the Cappadocian analogy of three men fail?
Ousia and hypostasis: the words for one.back: Three men are **separate beings acting separately**; the divine Persons share **one will, one action, one life**, and are one God.
"**Face, person**": suspected because Sabellius used it for a mask; later used alongside *hypostasis* for a real person.

Homoousios: of one essence with the Fath.back: "**Of the same essence**": Nicaea's (325) word for the Son's relation to the Father.

Homoousios: of one essence with the Fath.front: Arius: 'there was when He was not'
Homoousios: of one essence with the Fath.back: Alexandrian priest (about **256–336**): the Son is a creature; "**there was when He was not**". Condemned at Nicaea.
"**Of a like essence**": the compromise term, differing by one iota; it left room for the Son to be less than God.
Bishop of Alexandria (about **296–373**), exiled five times for Nicaea; feasts **18 January** and **2 May**.

The Cappadocian Fathers and the settleme.back: **Basil the Great** (about 330–379), **Gregory the Theologian** (about 329–390), **Gregory of Nyssa** (about 335–395).
Anomoean (died about **394**) who held that God's essence is **unbegottenness**, and claimed to know it; answered by Basil and Gregory of Nyssa.
"**Fighters against the Spirit**": accepted the Son's divinity, denied the Spirit's; answered at Constantinople (381).

The Cappadocian Fathers and the settleme.front: Constantinople I (381) and the article on the Spirit
The Cappadocian Fathers and the settleme.back: Second Ecumenical Council: **completed the Creed**, confessed the Spirit **worshipped and glorified with the Father and Son**.

Begotten and proceeding: what distinguis.back: The hypostatic properties: the Father **unbegotten**, the Son **begotten**, the Spirit **proceeding**.

Begotten and proceeding: what distinguis.front: How do the divine Persons differ?
Begotten and proceeding: what distinguis.back: **Only in their relations of origin**, never in what they are: all else (goodness, power, will, glory) is common.

Begotten and proceeding: what distinguis.front: In what sense is the Father "greater" (John 14:28)?
Begotten and proceeding: what distinguis.back: **As cause, not in nature**: "from him flows both the Equality and the Being of the Equals" (Gregory, Oration 40).

Reading: St Gregory the Theologian, Thir.front: Gregory's "Monarchy that is not limited to one Person" (Oration 29)
Reading: St Gregory the Theologian, Thir.back: One God, one source, but **not a solitary Person**: equality of nature, union of mind, identity of motion among the Three.

Reading: St Gregory the Theologian, Thir.front: "They are above all When": Gregory's answer to Arius
Reading: St Gregory the Theologian, Thir.back: The Three are eternal: "**There never was a time when He was not**", Arius' slogan turned round.

Reading: St Gregory the Theologian, Thir.front: Gregory's image of the sun and its light
Reading: St Gregory the Theologian, Thir.back: "**The sun is not prior to its light**": the Son and Spirit are from the Father but not after Him.

One will, one action: perichoresis and t.back: "**Interpenetration**": each Person of the Trinity dwells in the others without confusion or separation (John of Damascus).

One will, one action: perichoresis and t.front: Why do the Fathers say there are not three gods? (Gregory of Nyssa)
One will, one action: perichoresis and t.back: Because every divine action **begins with the Father, passes through the Son and is completed in the Spirit**: one action, not three.

One will, one action: perichoresis and t.front: "I see but one torch": Gregory, Oration 40
One will, one action: perichoresis and t.back: Thinking the One he is illumined by the Three; distinguishing the Three he is carried back to the One: **"the Undivided Light"**.

The procession of the Holy Spirit and th.front: Filioque: the Western addition to the Creed
The procession of the Holy Spirit and th.back: Latin "**and from the Son**", added to the Creed in the West (Spain, 6th century; Rome about **1014**). Not accepted by the Orthodox Church.

The procession of the Holy Spirit and th.front: What does the Orthodox Church teach about the Spirit's origin?
The procession of the Holy Spirit and th.back: **The Spirit proceeds from the Father alone** as single source, rests on the Son, and **shines forth and is sent through the Son**.
Under **Gregory of Cyprus**: distinguished the Spirit's **eternal origin** from the Father from His **eternal manifestation through the Son**.

Errors the Church rejected about the Tri.back: One God appearing in **three modes or masks**; denies the three real Persons. Early 3rd century.
**Three separate gods** sharing a kind of nature; rejected, e.g. when charged against John Philoponus (6th century).

Errors the Church rejected about the Tri.front: Why were the Trinitarian errors attractive?
Errors the Church rejected about the Tri.back: Each **made the faith simpler**: modalism kept oneness tidy, Arianism kept God remote, tritheism made the Persons easy to picture.

Apophatic theology: knowing God by unkno.back: *Apophasis*, "negation": speaking of God by **saying what He is not**, since no created concept fits Him.

Apophatic theology: knowing God by unkno.front: John of Damascus on what can be grasped of God
Apophatic theology: knowing God by unkno.back: "**All that is comprehensible about Him is His infinity and incomprehensibility**" (*Exposition* 1.4).
**No.** True statements about God point beyond themselves; apophasis is humility that leads **to the living Trinity and to worship**.

Cataphatic theology: the names of God.back: *Kataphasis*, "affirmation": speaking of God by **the names He has revealed**: good, wise, love, light.

Cataphatic theology: the names of God.front: Affirm, deny, exceed: the three steps of Dionysius
Cataphatic theology: the names of God.back: God is wise; **not** wise as creatures are; **beyond** wisdom, its source.
"**Condescension**": God speaking in human terms (hand, eyes, anger) so that we can understand.

Essence and energies: God unknown and kn.back: God's **uncreated energies**: His real presence and action toward creation (grace, light, life, love), distinct from His unknowable essence.
"**His operations come down to us, but His essence remains beyond our reach.**"

Essence and energies: God unknown and kn.front: St Gregory Palamas and the hesychasts
Essence and energies: God unknown and kn.back: Monk of Athos, Archbishop of Thessalonica (**1296–1359**); defended the hesychasts. Upheld by councils of **1341, 1347, 1351**. Feast: second Sunday of Lent and 14 November.

Essence and energies: God unknown and kn.front: Why does the essence–energies distinction matter?
Essence and energies: God unknown and kn.back: It keeps **God's transcendence** (we never share His essence) and **real union** (grace is God Himself, uncreated), without dividing God.

Creation from nothing.back: **Creation from nothing**: God gave existence itself, not form to an eternal matter (2 Maccabees 7:28).

Creation from nothing.front: How does creating differ from begetting? (John of Damascus)
Creation from nothing.back: Begetting is **the work of nature**, from the Father's essence, eternal; creation is **the work of will**, from nothing, with a beginning.
**Not from need but out of goodness and love**, so that others might share His goodness.

Created and uncreated: the great divide.back: **Uncreated** (God: essence and energies) and **created** (everything else, angels and souls included).

Created and uncreated: the great divide.front: Are souls or angels divine by being spiritual?
Created and uncreated: the great divide.back: **No.** They are creatures from nothing like stones; the line runs between **uncreated and created**, not spirit and matter.

Created and uncreated: the great divide.front: Why do the Fathers reject emanation?
Created and uncreated: the great divide.back: Creatures **do not flow out of God's essence**; between God and the highest angel there is no slope, only the gulf crossed by **God's free love**.

The invisible creation: the angels.back: "Messenger": "**an intelligent essence, in perpetual motion, with free-will, incorporeal, ministering to God**", immortal by grace (John of Damascus).
Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones; Dominions, Powers, Authorities; Principalities, Archangels, Angels (**Dionysius**, *Celestial Hierarchy*). A theologoumenon.

The invisible creation: the angels.front: Synaxis of the Archangel Michael (8 November)
The invisible creation: the angels.back: Feast of **Michael and all the bodiless powers**; Mondays are also dedicated to the angels.

The human person: made in the image and.back: **Image** (εἰκών): what is given, mind and freedom. **Likeness** (ὁμοίωσις): what is attained, virtue and union with God.

The human person: made in the image and.front: Is the image of God lost by sin?

The human person: made in the image and.back: "**Little world**": man unites visible and invisible creation, body from earth and soul from God's breath, and is called to offer creation to God.

Providence: God's care for his creation.back: **Providence**: "the care that God takes over existing things" (John of Damascus).

Providence: God's care for his creation.front: Good pleasure and permission in God's providence
Providence: God's care for his creation.back: *Eudokia*: what God **wills** (all good). *Synchoresis*: what He **permits** (free creatures' evil choices) without willing it.

Providence: God's care for his creation.front: Does God's foreknowledge cause our choices?
Providence: God's care for his creation.back: **No.** God foreknows but **does not predetermine** free choices; the Church rejects predestination to damnation.

Looking back: God and the Trinity.front: The doctrine of God in one sentence
Looking back: God and the Trinity.back: **One God, the Father, eternally begetting the Son and bringing forth the Spirit, one essence in three hypostases, unknowable in essence, known in uncreated energies, Creator of all from nothing.**

Looking back: God and the Trinity.front: Four questions on which Orthodox writers differ (Stage 2)
Looking back: God and the Trinity.back: The gravity of the **filioque** as doctrine; how to describe the **essence–energies** distinction; how far to build **personhood** on the Trinity; **Genesis and science**.

Context: the second article of the Creed.front: Who is Jesus Christ, in one sentence?
Context: the second article of the Creed.back: **The eternal Son of God, one of the Holy Trinity, who became truly man without ceasing to be God, so that man might be united to God.**
In Christology, *oikonomia* (οἰκονομία) is **God's saving plan**, above all the Incarnation; distinguished from *theologia*, God in Himself.

Context: the second article of the Creed.front: Why did the Fathers fight over who Christ is?
Context: the second article of the Creed.back: Because **salvation depends on it**: not God, He cannot unite us to God; not man, He has not united *us*; two persons, God and man only stand side by side.

The fall: what happened in Paradise.front: Was Adam created perfect, according to St Irenaeus?
The fall: what happened in Paradise.back: **Good but not yet perfect**: like a child meant to grow into God's likeness. The fall turned aside from that growth.

The fall: what happened in Paradise.front: Why does turning from God bring death?
The fall: what happened in Paradise.back: Because **God is life**; to turn from Him is to turn toward death, like a branch cut from the vine.
"**The first gospel**": Genesis 3:15, the promise that the woman's seed will strike the serpent; read as Christ's victory.

Ancestral sin: what we inherit from Adam.back: "**Ancestral sin**": the preferred modern Orthodox term; we inherit **death and corruption** from Adam, not his personal guilt.

Ancestral sin: what we inherit from Adam.front: What do all Orthodox hold about the effects of Adam's sin?
Ancestral sin: what we inherit from Adam.back: All are born **mortal and subject to corruption**, with a **wounded nature** inclined to sin; the image remains; **each sins freely**; baptism heals.

Ancestral sin: what we inherit from Adam.front: Two Orthodox emphases on ancestral sin
Ancestral sin: what we inherit from Adam.back: **Romanides, Meyendorff**: inherited mortality, not guilt. **Older catechisms (Mogila 1640, Philaret 1823)**: "original sin", a real inherited sinful condition. Neither makes infants guilty of Adam's act.
Greek **ἐφ᾽ ᾧ**: read in Latin as "in whom (Adam) all sinned"; by many Greek Fathers as "**because all sinned**".

Death and corruption: St Athanasius on t.back: **Corruption**: decay toward non-existence. For Athanasius the human problem is **a mortal disease**, not first a legal debt.

Death and corruption: St Athanasius on t.front: Why was repentance not enough, according to Athanasius?
Death and corruption: St Athanasius on t.back: Repentance **stays acts of sin but does not call nature back from corruption**; nature itself had to be restored.
God's **goodness** forbids letting His work waste away; His **truth** forbids revoking the sentence of death. Only the Word's Incarnation resolves both.

The promise: Christ foretold in the Old.back: "**Behold, a virgin (parthenos) shall conceive in the womb**... and thou shalt call his name **Emmanuel**" ("God with us").
A **type**: a person, event or thing that foreshadows Christ (Isaac, the Passover lamb, Jonah, the bronze serpent).

The promise: Christ foretold in the Old.front: Name three Old Testament types of the Theotokos

\"One Lord Jesus Christ\": the names and.back: "**Jesus Christ conquers**": the letters on the Eucharistic bread; IC XC are the first and last letters of *Iesous Christos*.
"**Only-begotten**": the unique Son of the Father, not one son among many.

The eternal Word: \"In the beginning was.back: "**Word**": the eternal Son, who "was with God, and... was God" (John 1:1); a Person, not an impersonal principle.

The eternal Word: \"In the beginning was.front: Who appeared in the Old Testament theophanies, according to the Fathers?
The eternal Word: \"In the beginning was.back: **The Word before His Incarnation**, to Abraham, Moses and Isaiah; hence *ho On* on Christ's halo.

\"Was incarnate and was made man\": the.front: Why does the Creed add "was made man" to "was incarnate"?
\"Was incarnate and was made man\": the.back: "Flesh" could be misread as a body only; **"was made man"** says He became **a complete human being**, body, soul and mind.
"**Self-emptying**" (Philippians 2:7): the Word humbling Himself to take the form of a servant, **without giving up His divinity**.
Hymn sung at every Liturgy, attributed to **Emperor Justinian** (6th century): the Son, incarnate of the ever-virgin Theotokos "without change of essence", "one of the Holy Trinity".
Gabriel's message to Mary and the **conception of Christ**; Mary's "be it unto me according to thy word".

Why God became man: St Athanasius and St.front: Irenaeus on why the Word became man (Against Heresies 5, preface)
Why God became man: St Athanasius and St.back: He "**became what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself**".
**Recapitulation** (Irenaeus): Christ, the new Adam, sums up human life and **undoes Adam's disobedience by His obedience**.

Why God became man: St Athanasius and St.front: Would the Word have become man without the fall?
Why God became man: St Athanasius and St.back: **Orthodox writers differ**: some, following hints in Maximus, say union was God's purpose from the start; others call the question idle. Both put God's love first.

Reading: St Athanasius, On the Incarnati.front: On the Incarnation of the Word
Reading: St Athanasius, On the Incarnati.back: St Athanasius' early treatise (between about **318 and the 330s**) on why the Word became man; tr. Archibald Robertson, NPNF 2/4 (1892).

Reading: St Athanasius, On the Incarnati.front: "He was made man that we might be made God" (On the Incarnation 54)
Reading: St Athanasius, On the Incarnati.back: The purpose of the Incarnation is **theosis**: sharing by grace in God's life, not becoming God by nature.

Reading: St Athanasius, On the Incarnati.front: Athanasius' image of the king in the city (section 9)
Reading: St Athanasius, On the Incarnati.back: As a king dwelling in **one house** protects **the whole city**, so the Word dwelling in **one body** protects the whole human race.

Truly God: the divinity of Christ.front: Why must Christ be God, according to Athanasius?
Truly God: the divinity of Christ.back: **A creature cannot give what it does not have by nature**; only God can unite us to God.
Christ "who was crucified in the flesh is **true God and the Lord of Glory and one of the Holy Trinity**".

Truly man: a human body, soul and mind.front: Apollinarianism and the human mind of Christ
Truly man: a human body, soul and mind.back: Teaching of **Apollinaris of Laodicea** (about 310–390): the Word replaced Christ's human mind. Condemned at **Constantinople (381)**.

Truly man: a human body, soul and mind.front: Gregory to Cledonius: not assumed, not healed
Truly man: a human body, soul and mind.back: St Gregory the Theologian (Letter 101): **whatever part of our nature Christ did not take, He did not heal**; so He took body, soul, mind and will.
From *dokeo*, "**to seem**": Christ only seemed to have a body and suffer. Rejected from the apostles and Ignatius on.
**Hunger, tiredness, grief, fear of death**: natural human weaknesses Christ freely took on; distinct from sinful passions.

The Theotokos: Ephesus (431) and the Mot.back: "**She who gave birth to God**": Mary's title, defended at **Ephesus (431)**. ΜΡ ΘΥ on her icons.
Archbishop of Constantinople (from **428**) who preferred "**Christ-bearer**"; deposed at Ephesus (431).

The Theotokos: Ephesus (431) and the Mot.front: Why did St Cyril insist on Theotokos?
The Theotokos: Ephesus (431) and the Mot.back: If Mary did not bear God, **the one she bore was not God**, and Christ would be **two subjects**, two sons.
The hymn to the Theotokos sung at every Liturgy: "**thou who without defilement barest God the Word, true Birth-giver of God, we magnify thee**".

The Ever-Virgin Mary in Orthodox teachin.back: "**Ever-virgin**": Mary a virgin **before, during and after** Christ's birth; the title used by Constantinople II (553).
"**All-holy**": the Church's title for the Theotokos; common Orthodox teaching holds she **never committed personal sin**.
*Koimesis*, "**falling asleep**": Mary truly died and was **taken up in body**; universal tradition in the services, not a conciliar dogma.

The Ever-Virgin Mary in Orthodox teachin.front: The four great feasts of the Theotokos and their dates

The Definition of Chalcedon (451): one p.back: Archimandrite of Constantinople (about **380–456**): after the union **one nature only**. Condemned at **Chalcedon (451)**.

The Definition of Chalcedon (451): one p.front: The four adverbs of Chalcedon and the errors they exclude
Trinity and Christ: natures and persons
The Definition of Chalcedon (451): one p.back: **Trinity**: one nature, three persons. **Christ**: two natures, one person.
*Homoousios* **with the Father** in His Godhead, *homoousios* **with us** in His manhood.

The hypostatic union and the exchange of.back: The **union of divine and human natures in the one hypostasis of God the Word**: not two persons by agreement, nor a mixture.
The **exchange of properties** (*communicatio idiomatum*): what belongs to either nature is said of the one Person, so "**God died in the flesh**".
"**Existing in a hypostasis**": Christ's humanity is complete but exists **in the Person of the Word**, not as a separate human person.

The hypostatic union and the exchange of.front: Iron in the fire: what the image shows of Christ
The hypostatic union and the exchange of.back: Christ's humanity is **penetrated by the divine energy and glorified**, as iron glows with fire, yet **remains human**.

Two wills and two energies: St Maximus a.back: From *thelema*, "will": **one will in Christ**; imperial doctrine in the **Ekthesis (638)**; condemned at **Constantinople III (680–681)**.

Two wills and two energies: St Maximus a.front: St Maximus the Confessor and the two wills
Two wills and two energies: St Maximus a.back: Monk (about **580–662**); **will belongs to nature**, so Christ has two wills; mutilated and exiled for it. Feasts **21 January** and 13 August.
Christ's **human will**, shrinking from death, **freely submits** to the divine will, which is His own as God.
The **deliberating, hesitating** choice of a person who does not see the good clearly; **Christ has a natural human will but no gnomic will**.

Christ revealed: the Nativity and the Tr.back: On **Mount Tabor** Christ shone before Peter, James and John, with Moses and Elijah; grapes and fruit are blessed.

Christ revealed: the Nativity and the Tr.front: Why were the disciples shown the Transfiguration, according to its kontakion?
Christ revealed: the Nativity and the Tr.back: "**That when they should see thee crucified they might comprehend that thy suffering was voluntary.**"

Christ revealed: the Nativity and the Tr.front: Was the light of Tabor created?
Christ revealed: the Nativity and the Tr.back: **No**: the **uncreated glory of God** shining through Christ's humanity; the disciples' eyes were opened "in so far as they were able".

The Cross: the voluntary Passion.back: Roman prefect of Judaea **26–36**; named in the Creed to fix the crucifixion in history (about **AD 30 or 33**).
"**It is finished**" (John 19:30): the work brought to its goal.

The Cross: the voluntary Passion.front: Exaltation of the Cross (14 September) and St Helen
The Cross: the voluntary Passion.back: Recalls the **finding of the Cross by St Helen** in Jerusalem (4th century); a strict fast day.

Ransom, sacrifice, victory and healing:.front: To whom was the ransom paid, according to Gregory the Theologian (Oration 45)?
Ransom, sacrifice, victory and healing:.back: **Neither to the devil nor to the Father as a demand**: the Father "accepts Him, but neither asked for Him nor demanded Him"; humanity had to be sanctified by God's humanity.

Ransom, sacrifice, victory and healing:.front: How do Orthodox writers treat legal language for the Cross?
Ransom, sacrifice, victory and healing:.back: **Some reject juridical theories** (Antony Khrapovitsky, Romanides); **others keep legal language in its place** (Athanasius: "satisfied the debt"). All: the Cross is **God's love**, not appeasement.

The descent into Hades.back: The **realm of the dead** (Hebrew *Sheol*) where all who died before Christ awaited Him; not the final hell.
The Orthodox **icon of the Resurrection**: Christ on the broken gates of Hades **raising Adam and Eve by the wrists**.

The descent into Hades.front: Whom did Christ free in Hades?
The descent into Hades.back: **The righteous of the Old Testament** for certain; how widely His preaching saved is **not defined**, and the Fathers differ.

The Resurrection on the third day.front: How does Christ's Resurrection differ from Lazarus' raising?
The Resurrection on the third day.back: Lazarus returned to mortal life and died again; **Christ rose in a glorified body and "dieth no more"** (Romans 6:9).

The Resurrection on the third day.front: Pascha (Πάσχα): the name of the feast
The Resurrection on the third day.back: From Hebrew *Pesach*, **Passover**: the feast of the Resurrection, "the feast of feasts".
"**Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down Death by death, and upon those in the tomb bestowing life.**"
The first **witnesses of the empty tomb**; their Sunday is two weeks after Pascha. St Mary Magdalene is "**equal to the apostles**".

Salvation in Orthodox teaching: grace, f.back: **Grace**: God's own **uncreated energy**, His life given to us; not a created substance.
**Grace and freedom work together**: God works "both to will and to do"; we consent and keep turning, like a sick man taking medicine he could never make.

Salvation in Orthodox teaching: grace, f.front: Have we been saved, are we being saved, or shall we be saved?
Salvation in Orthodox teaching: grace, f.back: **All three**: in baptism, through the life of the Church, and at the resurrection and judgement.

Theosis: becoming by grace what God is b.back: **Deification**: participation of the whole person **in the life of God by grace**, remaining a creature (2 Peter 1:4).

Theosis: becoming by grace what God is b.front: "By grace, not by nature": the rule of theosis
Theosis: becoming by grace what God is b.back: **We become by grace what God is by nature**; we never share His essence or become a person of the Trinity.
"**Stretching forward**" (Gregory of Nyssa): union with the infinite God is **eternal growth**, without end.

Theosis without confusion: union with Go.front: Why is theosis not absorption into God?
Theosis without confusion: union with Go.back: We are united to God **in His energies, never His essence**, on the pattern of Christ's two natures **without confusion**; the person remains.

Theosis without confusion: union with Go.front: Iron in the fire: what the image shows of theosis
Theosis without confusion: union with Go.back: Iron in fire **glows and burns like fire but remains iron**; so the deified person shines with God's light and remains human.

Theosis without confusion: union with Go.front: St Silouan the Athonite and love for enemies
Theosis without confusion: union with Go.back: Russian monk of Athos (**1866–1938**), canonised **1987**: **love for enemies** as the test of the Spirit's presence.

Christ the Prophet, Priest and King.back: **Prophet** (reveals the Father, is the Word), **Priest** (offers Himself, intercedes), **King** (rules all; His kingdom has no end).
From the priest's prayer at the Cherubic Hymn: **Christ is both the priest and the offering**.

Christ the Prophet, Priest and King.front: How does every Christian share Christ's three offices?
Christ the Prophet, Priest and King.back: Anointed at chrismation: **prophet** by confessing the faith, **priest** by offering prayer and life, **king** by ruling the passions (1 Peter 2:9).

The Ascension and the Second Coming.front: The Ascension: our nature borne to the Father
The Ascension and the Second Coming.back: **Thursday, forty days after Pascha**: Christ taken up from the Mount of Olives, **bearing our nature** to the Father.
"**Presence, arrival**": Christ's **Second Coming in glory** to judge the living and the dead.

The Ascension and the Second Coming.front: Is the Ascension Christ's absence, according to its kontakion?
The Ascension and the Second Coming.back: **No**: "**in no wise departing but abiding uninterruptedly with us**", in the Spirit and the Eucharist.
Added at **Constantinople (381)** against **Marcellus of Ancyra**, who taught Christ's reign would end.

Looking back: Christ.back: **One Person, the eternal Son, in two natures, divine and human, unconfused and undivided, with two wills in harmony; made man that we might be made god by grace.**

Looking back: Christ.front: What each council from 325 to 681 said about Christ
Looking back: Christ.back: **Nicaea**: truly God. **Constantinople I**: truly man, with a human mind. **Ephesus**: Theotokos. **Chalcedon**: two natures. **Constantinople II**: one of the Trinity. **Constantinople III**: two wills.

Context: the third part of the Creed.back: The Creed of **Nicaea (325)** as expanded by **Constantinople I (381)**, which added the article on the Spirit and those after it. Text fixed since 381; recited without addition.
The Orthodox name for the Creed. A *symbolon* was a token broken in two, matched to prove identity.
**8** the Holy Spirit; **9** the Church; **10** one Baptism; **11** the resurrection of the dead; **12** the life of the world to come.

The Holy Spirit in the Creed: \"the Lord.back: "**Fighters against the Spirit**": 4th-century party that accepted the Son's divinity but made the Spirit a creature. Answered by **Constantinople I (381)**.

The Holy Spirit in the Creed: \"the Lord.front: How does the Creed of 381 show the Spirit is God?
The Holy Spirit in the Creed: \"the Lord.back: It calls him **Lord** and **Giver of Life**, and says he is **worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son**. Only God is worshipped.
John's title for the Spirit (John 14:16): **Comforter, advocate, helper**, one called alongside.

The Holy Spirit in the Creed: \"the Lord.front: Why is "O heavenly King" not said from Pascha to Pentecost?
The Holy Spirit in the Creed: \"the Lord.back: It is the prayer to the Spirit; the Church **waits for the Spirit** until Pentecost, as the apostles did.

The Spirit in the Old Testament and the.front: St Gregory the Theologian on why the Spirit was revealed last
The Spirit in the Old Testament and the.back: Oration 31.26 (380): the OT showed the Father openly and the Son obscurely; the NT the Son, and suggested the Spirit; **now the Spirit dwells among us**. Revelation came step by step, as people could bear it.
Given by Orthodoxy to **three saints**: John the Evangelist, Gregory of Nazianzus, Symeon the New Theologian.

Pentecost: the feast and the event.back: "Fiftieth": **50 days after Pascha**; the descent of the Spirit (Acts 2); one of the twelve great feasts; called **Trinity Sunday** in Slavic use.
Vespers of Pentecost Sunday evening: **the first kneeling since Pascha**, with three long prayers attributed to St Basil.
At Babel God **divided** the nations by confusing tongues; at Pentecost tongues of fire **call all to unity**. The languages remain, now carrying one faith.
The crowned old man in the dark arch below the apostles: **the world, awaiting the apostles' preaching**.

The procession of the Spirit and the fil.back: Latin "**and from the Son**", added to the Creed in the West: Toledo **589**, adopted in Rome **1014**. Not in the Orthodox Creed.
The Father as **the one source** (*aitía*) of the Son (by generation) and of the Spirit (by procession).

The procession of the Spirit and the fil.front: Procession versus sending of the Spirit
The procession of the Spirit and the fil.back: **Procession** (*ekpóreusis*): eternal origin, **from the Father**. **Sending**: mission into the world in time, **from the Father through the Son** (John 15:26).
Treatise of **St Photios** of Constantinople, about **886**, setting out the Orthodox case against the filioque.

Acquiring the Holy Spirit: gifts and fru.back: Russian monk and elder, **1754–1833** (some say born 1759); glorified **1903**. Conversation with **Motovilov, November 1831**: the aim of the Christian life is **acquiring the Holy Spirit**.

Acquiring the Holy Spirit: gifts and fru.front: Gifts (charísmata) versus fruit (karpós) of the Spirit
Acquiring the Holy Spirit: gifts and fru.back: Gifts are abilities **distributed** for service, and can exist without holiness; fruit (Galatians 5:22–23: love, joy, peace...) is **Christ's character formed in us**, meant for all.
"**Working together**": God's grace saves, and human freedom must cooperate with it.

Reading: St Basil, On the Holy Spirit 9,.front: St Basil, On the Holy Spirit (375)
Reading: St Basil, On the Holy Spirit 9,.back: Written for **Amphilochius of Iconium**, sparked by Basil's doxology "with the Son together with the Holy Spirit"; prepared the ground for **381**.

Reading: St Basil, On the Holy Spirit 9,.front: Basil's image of the sunbeam and glass: what it teaches
Reading: St Basil, On the Holy Spirit 9,.back: Glass in sunlight shines with **the sun's light, not its own**: the soul is made god **by grace and participation**, not by nature.

Reading: St Basil, On the Holy Spirit 9,.front: Basil's argument that the Spirit is God, from deification
Reading: St Basil, On the Holy Spirit 9,.back: Only God can make someone god. **The Spirit deifies, so the Spirit is God.**

The Church as the Body of Christ.back: Greek "**assembly**", from *ek-kaléō*, "call out": the people God has called together.

The Church as the Body of Christ.front: St Irenaeus on the Church and the Spirit (Against Heresies III.24.1)
The Church as the Body of Christ.back: "For **where the Church is, there is the Spirit of God**; and where the Spirit of God is, there is the Church, and every kind of grace."
*On the Unity of the Church* §6: "He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not **the Church for his mother**."

The Church as the Body of Christ.front: What does the Church teach about those outside her bounds?
The Church as the Body of Christ.back: **Salvation is given in the Church.** Most Orthodox writers add: we know where the Church is, not where she is not; God judges those outside. Not defined.

One, holy, catholic and apostolic: the f.back: From *kath' hólou*, "**according to the whole**": lacking nothing, and for all. First used by **St Ignatius of Antioch** (*Smyrnaeans* 8, about 107).

One, holy, catholic and apostolic: the f.front: How is the Church holy when her members sin?
One, holy, catholic and apostolic: the f.back: She is holy by **Christ her head and the Spirit in her**, not by sinless members: a hospital (Chrysostom's image) full of the sick.

One, holy, catholic and apostolic: the f.front: The three ways the Church is apostolic
One, holy, catholic and apostolic: the f.back: In **faith** (the apostles' teaching), **succession** (bishops ordained from the apostles), and **mission** (sent to all nations).

Bishops, apostolic succession and the eu.back: **Bishop** (overseer), **priest** (elder), **deacon** (servant): the threefold ministry, universal by the early 2nd century.

Bishops, apostolic succession and the eu.front: What is apostolic succession in Orthodox teaching?
Bishops, apostolic succession and the eu.back: An unbroken line of ordination **together with the apostolic faith and a real local church**; not a mechanical chain of hands.
The view, developed by **Afanasiev** and **Zizioulas**, that each local church gathered round its bishop at the Eucharist is the whole Church.
"**Self-headed**": a church that elects its own primate.

Conciliarity: sobornost and the councils.back: Russian "**conciliarity**" (from *sobor*, council): the Church's free unity in which truth is held by the whole body. Made famous by **Khomiakov (1804–1860)**.
The apostles' council on Gentile converts; its formula: "**it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us**".
Not size or who summoned it, but **reception**: the whole Church receives its teaching as the faith she has always held. Orthodoxy recognises **seven** (325–787).

The Mysteries: what a sacrament is in Or.back: Greek "**mystery**": something hidden now revealed. Latin *sacramentum*. The Orthodox name for a sacrament.

The Mysteries: what a sacrament is in Or.front: Why does God give grace through matter?
The Mysteries: what a sacrament is in Or.back: Because of **the Incarnation**: the Word took flesh, so water, oil, bread, wine and hands can carry divine life.

The Mysteries: what a sacrament is in Or.front: Who is the true celebrant of the Mysteries?
The Mysteries: what a sacrament is in Or.back: **Christ.** The priest's prayer: "it is thou who offerest and art offered"; baptism says "the servant of God **is baptized**".

How many Mysteries? Seven, and the sacra.back: **Baptism, chrismation, Eucharist, confession, marriage, holy unction, holy orders.**

How many Mysteries? Seven, and the sacra.front: Where did the number seven come from?
How many Mysteries? Seven, and the sacra.back: Not counted by the early Fathers; common from the **13th century**; fixed in **Mogila's Confession (1643)** and the **Synod of Jerusalem (1672)**.
Writer of **about 500**: illumination, synaxis, myron, ordination, **monastic tonsure**, the rites for the dead.

Baptism: dying and rising with Christ.back: Greek "**I plunge, immerse**". Orthodox baptism is by **threefold immersion**; also called *phōtismós*, **Illumination**.
The fallen condition, **mortality and corruption**, inherited from Adam. Most Orthodox writers deny that infants bear personal guilt for it.

Baptism: dying and rising with Christ.front: Who may baptise in danger of death?
Baptism: dying and rising with Christ.back: **Any Orthodox Christian**, with threefold immersion or pouring and the words of the rite. A priest completes the rest if the person lives.
**Godparent, sponsor**: answers for an infant at baptism and promises to raise them in the faith.

The rite of baptism step by step.front: Why does the person face west, then east, at baptism?
The rite of baptism step by step.back: **West**, the direction of darkness: **renouncing Satan**. **East**, toward the rising sun: **uniting with Christ** and reciting the Creed.

The rite of baptism step by step.front: The order of the Orthodox baptismal rite
The rite of baptism step by step.back: Catechumen prayers, **exorcisms**, **renunciation**, union with Christ and Creed, blessing of water, oil of gladness, **threefold immersion**, white robe, **chrismation**, procession, tonsure, **Communion**.

Chrismation: the seal of the gift of the.back: Olive oil, wine and **dozens of aromatics**, consecrated in Holy Week by the **primate** of an autocephalous church.
At each anointing: "**The seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit. Amen.**"

Chrismation: the seal of the gift of the.front: Why does Orthodoxy give baptism, chrismation and Communion together?
Chrismation: the seal of the gift of the.back: They are **one initiation**: born, given the Spirit's breath, then fed. Infants receive all three on the same day.

Receiving converts: akriveia and oikonom.back: "**Exactness, strictness**": applying the canons and the norm in full.
"**Stewardship**": a bishop's pastoral relaxation of the strict norm for the salvation of souls, **without changing the teaching**.

Receiving converts: akriveia and oikonom.front: How are converts received into the Orthodox Church?
Receiving converts: akriveia and oikonom.back: By **baptism**, **chrismation**, or **confession of faith**. Practice differs: Constantinople (**1755**) required baptism of Latins; Moscow (**1667**) received them by chrismation. The bishop decides.

The Eucharist: the Mystery of the Church.back: Greek "**thanksgiving**", from Christ's giving thanks at the Last Supper.
"**Change**": the Fathers' word for the bread and wine becoming Christ's Body and Blood.

The Eucharist: the Mystery of the Church.front: What does the Church teach about the Eucharistic change?
The Eucharist: the Mystery of the Church.back: The Gifts **truly become** Christ's Body and Blood, at the **epiclesis** within the anaphora. The manner is a mystery; Jerusalem (1672) used *metousiōsis*, many modern writers say simply "change".

The Eucharist: the Mystery of the Church.front: Why do Orthodox Christians receive Communion only in the Orthodox Church?
The Eucharist: the Mystery of the Church.back: **Communion with Christ is communion with one another** (1 Corinthians 10:17): the common cup expresses an existing unity of faith.

The communion of saints.back: **Equal-to-the-Apostles**: saints who brought whole peoples to Christ (Nino, Cyril and Methodius, Vladimir, Constantine and Helen).
A church's **synodal recognition** of a saint, after examining life, veneration and miracles. Paisios: Constantinople, **2015**.

The communion of saints.front: Do death and the grave break the Church?
The communion of saints.back: No: God "is not the God of the dead, but of the living". **The Church on earth and in heaven is one**, and all pray for all.

The Theotokos and the saints in prayer:.back: **Latreia**: worship, **God alone**. **Proskynesis**: veneration, given to saints, icons, relics, the Cross. Distinguished by **Nicaea II (787)**.

The Theotokos and the saints in prayer:.front: Why is the Theotokos honoured above all creatures?
The Theotokos and the saints in prayer:.back: She is the one **in whom God became man**: "More honourable than the Cherubim, and beyond compare more glorious than the Seraphim".
The cloth on which the Liturgy is served, with **relics of a martyr** sewn into it, signed by the bishop.

Death and the departure of the soul.front: What is death, in Orthodox teaching?
Death and the departure of the soul.back: **The separation of soul from body**, which God made one. It is **not natural** to humanity as created, but "the last enemy" Christ has overcome.

Death and the departure of the soul.front: Is the soul immortal by nature?
Death and the departure of the soul.back: Orthodox teaching: **not by its own nature but by God's gift**, and Christian hope is the **resurrection of the whole person**, not just an immortal soul.
"**Falling asleep**": the Christian word for death in hope of resurrection; hence *koimētḗrion*, cemetery.

The intermediate state and prayer for th.back: After death each soul receives **a foretaste** of its final state. Distinct from the **general judgement** at the Second Coming.
"**Saturdays of souls**": memorial Saturdays before Meatfare Sunday, before Pentecost, and in Lent.

The intermediate state and prayer for th.front: Memorial days after an Orthodox death
The intermediate state and prayer for th.back: **3rd, 9th and 40th days**, then anniversaries; with **kollyva** (boiled wheat) and "Memory eternal".

The intermediate state and prayer for th.front: St Mark of Ephesus at Florence (1438–39)
The intermediate state and prayer for th.back: Set out the Orthodox view: the departed are helped by **prayer and God's mercy**, **without a purgatorial fire**.

The toll-houses: a question among Orthod.back: The teaching that after death the soul passes **demonic accusers in the air**, answered by angels. **Not defined by any council.**

The toll-houses: a question among Orthod.front: The toll-houses: who holds the teaching, and why
The toll-houses: a question among Orthod.back: **Ignatius Brianchaninov, Theophan the Recluse, John Maximovitch, Seraphim Rose** (*The Soul After Death*, 1980): long witness in Fathers, lives and services; it stresses repentance.

The toll-houses: a question among Orthod.front: The toll-houses: who rejects the teaching, and why
The toll-houses: a question among Orthod.back: **Lev (Lazar) Puhalo**, **Michael Azkoul**, and others: not in Scripture, Creed or councils; resting on visions; judgement belongs to Christ, not demons.

The toll-houses: a question among Orthod.front: The toll-houses: what both sides agree on
The toll-houses: a question among Orthod.back: A **particular judgement**; **repentance and Communion** prepare for it; **prayer helps** the departed; **Christ is the judge**.

The resurrection of the body and the Las.back: "**Presence, arrival**": the Second Coming of Christ. Orthodoxy **refuses to calculate its date**.

The resurrection of the body and the Las.front: What is the "spiritual body" of the resurrection?
The resurrection of the body and the Las.back: Not a ghost: **the same body, wholly filled by the Spirit**, transfigured and freed from death (1 Corinthians 15:44; Luke 24:39–43).

The resurrection of the body and the Las.front: By what measure does Christ judge in Matthew 25?
The resurrection of the body and the Las.back: **Love shown to Christ in "the least of these my brethren".** Read on **Meatfare Sunday**.

Heaven, hell and the hope for all.back: St Gregory of Nyssa's "**stretching forward**": endless growth into God, even in the Kingdom.

Heaven, hell and the hope for all.front: Heaven and hell as one reality, in many Orthodox writers
Heaven, hell and the hope for all.back: **God's love**, experienced as light by those who love him and as torment by those who refuse it. St Isaac the Syrian: the "scourge of love".
"**Restoration**" of all. The **Origenist** form was anathematised in connection with **Constantinople II (553)**; whether one may **hope** for all is debated among Orthodox writers.

Looking back: the Spirit, the Church and.back: **The same Spirit who spoke by the prophets** makes the Church, fills the font and the chalice, and will raise the dead.

Looking back: the Spirit, the Church and.front: Defined, taught by all, or open? Last things in Orthodox teaching
Looking back: the Spirit, the Church and.back: **Defined**: resurrection, Last Judgement. **Taught by all**: particular judgement, prayer for the dead, real hell. **Open**: toll-houses; hope for all.

Context: the Bible as the Church's book.front: What does the Church teach about Scripture and Tradition?
Context: the Bible as the Church's book.back: Scripture is **the highest written witness within Tradition**: not set against the Church, not beneath her. Both come from the same Spirit.

Context: the Bible as the Church's book.front: St Irenaeus's image of the king's portrait (Against Heresies I.8.1)
Context: the Bible as the Church's book.back: Heretics rearrange the jewels of a king's portrait into **a dog or a fox**: the pieces are Scripture, **the picture comes from the Church's faith**.

Context: the Bible as the Church's book.front: Why is the Gospel book kept on the altar?
Context: the Bible as the Church's book.back: Scripture is heard as **the voice of Christ in the assembly**; the Word read and the Word in the Eucharist are one Christ.

The canon of the Old Testament and the r.back: Greek "**rule, measuring rod**": the list of books received as the rule of faith.
"**The readable books**": Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, 1–3 Maccabees, additions to Esther and Daniel, 1 Esdras, Prayer of Manasseh, Psalm 151.

The canon of the Old Testament and the r.front: Are the readable books Scripture? The two Orthodox views
The canon of the Old Testament and the r.back: **Fully canonical**: Synod of Jerusalem (1672). **A second rank, read but not strictly canonical**: Athanasius (367), John of Damascus, Philaret. All read them in church.

The Septuagint: the Old Testament of the.back: The Greek Old Testament: the Torah translated in **Alexandria, 3rd century BC**, the rest over two centuries. The Bible of the apostles and the Orthodox Church.
The Hebrew text standardised by the **Masoretes, about 7th–10th centuries AD**; behind most modern translations.

The Septuagint: the Old Testament of the.front: Isaiah 7:14 in the Septuagint and the Hebrew
The Septuagint: the Old Testament of the.back: LXX: ***parthénos*, "virgin"** (the reading Matthew 1:23 follows). Hebrew: *ʿalmāh*, "young woman".

The Septuagint: the Old Testament of the.front: Why are Orthodox psalm numbers different?
The Septuagint: the Old Testament of the.back: The **Septuagint joins Psalms 9–10** (and splits 147), so from 10 to 147 its numbers are mostly **one lower**: LXX 50 = Hebrew 51.

The canon of the New Testament.back: The **first list of exactly the 27 New Testament books**: "These are fountains of salvation."

The canon of the New Testament.front: How did the Church recognise the New Testament books?
The canon of the New Testament.back: By **apostolic origin**, **agreement with the rule of faith**, and **use in the churches** from early on: recognition, not invention.

The canon of the New Testament.front: Why is Revelation not read in the Divine Liturgy?
The canon of the New Testament.back: It was **accepted late in the East**, after the Byzantine lectionary had formed, and was never added. Its authority is fully received.

Inspiration: the Spirit who spoke by the.front: What does the Church teach about how Scripture is inspired?
Inspiration: the Spirit who spoke by the.back: **God's word in fully human words**, like the Incarnation: a **synergy**, not dictation. The same Spirit inspires the writers, the Church's recognition and the reader.

The senses of Scripture: letter, type an.back: What the text says and what happened: **where every patristic reading begins**.
"**Contemplation**": perceiving the higher meaning the literal sense itself carries.

The senses of Scripture: letter, type an.front: Alexandria and Antioch: the two styles of patristic exegesis
The senses of Scripture: letter, type an.back: **Alexandria** (Origen, Cyril): open to allegory. **Antioch** (Diodore, Chrysostom, Theodoret): history, the plain sense and *theoria*. The Church kept both.
"**Leading up**": the sense of Scripture that points to the age to come.

Typology: how the Old Testament is read.back: A **type** is a real OT person or event that prefigures Christ or the Church; its fulfilment is the **antitype** (Romans 5:14; 1 Peter 3:21).

Typology: how the Old Testament is read.front: Five New Testament types of Christ
Typology: how the Old Testament is read.back: **Adam** (Romans 5), **Jonah** (Matthew 12:40), **the bronze serpent** (John 3:14), **the manna** (John 6), **the Passover lamb** (1 Corinthians 5:7).
The Orthodox name for the **Old Testament readings at Vespers**, chosen for their types.

Reading: Genesis 22 and St Augustine on.front: The types in Genesis 22 (the binding of Isaac)
Reading: Genesis 22 and St Augustine on.back: "**The beloved one**" (agapētós, as at Christ's baptism); **the third day**; **Isaac carrying the wood** (the Cross); **the ram caught by the horns** (Christ crowned with thorns, in Augustine).
The **tenth of the fifteen Old Testament readings** at the Vesperal Liturgy of Holy Saturday.
St Augustine's reading of Abraham's sacrifice: Isaac carried the wood "**just as the Lord Himself carried His own cross**" (tr. Dods, NPNF I.2, 1887).

Genesis: creation and the fall as the Ch.back: "**The first gospel**": Genesis 3:15, the first promise of Christ, the woman's seed who defeats the serpent.
Homilies on **the six days of creation**, reading the plain sense with the natural science of his time.

Genesis: creation and the fall as the Ch.front: What has the Church defined about Genesis 1–3, and what not?
Genesis: creation and the fall as the Ch.back: **Defined**: creation from nothing, its goodness, the image of God, the fall. **Not defined**: the age of the earth, evolution, how literally to read the days.

Moses and the Exodus in the Church's rea.back: "**The One who is**" (Exodus 3:14, Septuagint): written in the cross of **Christ's halo** in every icon.
**Passover lamb** = Christ; **Red Sea** = baptism; **manna and the rock** = the Eucharist and Christ; **burning bush** = the Theotokos.

The Psalter: the prayer book of the Chur.back: One of the **20 sections** of the Psalter, each in **three staseis**. The whole Psalter is read **weekly**, **twice a week in Lent**.
The **Six Psalms** at the start of Matins: **3, 37, 62, 87, 102, 142** (LXX), read in near darkness.

The Psalter: the prayer book of the Chur.front: Why do Christians pray the Psalms?
The Psalter: the prayer book of the Chur.back: They are **Christ's own prayer**, and they give words to **every movement of the soul** (Athanasius, *Letter to Marcellinus*, paraphrased).

The prophets and the Messiah.back: "**One who speaks for**" God: first a preacher of **repentance and justice**, and only partly a foreteller.
At the **Proskomedia** the priest cuts the Lamb saying "**He was led as a sheep to the slaughter**" (Isaiah 53:7).
"**God with us**" (Isaiah 7:14): sung at Great Compline of the Nativity and at weddings ("Rejoice, O Isaiah").

The Wisdom books: Proverbs, Job, Ecclesi.front: Who is Wisdom in Proverbs 8–9, in the Church's reading?
The Wisdom books: Proverbs, Job, Ecclesi.back: **The eternal Son and Word**, "Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24).
"The Lord **made** me the beginning of his ways": Arians took it of the Son's origin; **Athanasius read it of the Incarnation**.
The great church of Constantinople, named for **Holy Wisdom**, meaning Christ.

Types of the Theotokos in the Old Testam.front: Five Old Testament types of the Theotokos
Types of the Theotokos in the Old Testam.back: **Burning bush** (Exodus 3), **Jacob's ladder** (Genesis 28), **the closed gate** (Ezekiel 44), **Wisdom's house** (Proverbs 9), **Gideon's fleece** (Judges 6).

Types of the Theotokos in the Old Testam.front: The Vespers readings for feasts of the Theotokos

Types of the Theotokos in the Old Testam.back: Hymn to the Theotokos sung **standing** (*akáthistos*), probably 5th–6th century; **144 salutations**; sung in full on the **fifth Saturday of Lent**.

The four Gospels and why there are four.back: "**Good news**": one Gospel of Jesus Christ, in four accounts "according to" each evangelist.

The four Gospels and why there are four.front: The four evangelists' creatures, as usual in Orthodox icons today
The four Gospels and why there are four.back: **Matthew** man/angel, **Mark** lion, **Luke** ox, **John** eagle (Irenaeus gave the lion to John and the eagle to Mark).
Tatian's **harmony of the four Gospels into one**; used in Syriac churches for a time, then set aside.

The Synoptic Gospels: Matthew, Mark and.back: From *sýnopsis*, "**seeing together**": Matthew, Mark and Luke, which can be laid side by side.
Early 2nd century (in Eusebius III.39): Mark, "**the interpreter of Peter**", wrote down accurately what he remembered.

The Synoptic Gospels: Matthew, Mark and.front: The character of each Synoptic Gospel
The Synoptic Gospels: Matthew, Mark and.back: **Matthew**: for Jewish Christians, fulfilment, the new Moses. **Mark**: Peter's preaching, fast and vivid. **Luke**: mercy, and the Theotokos's side of the story.

The Gospel of John: the theologian's Gos.back: "**Word**" (also reason, meaning): John's name for the eternal Son, "made flesh" (John 1:14).
**Seven signs**, the **"I am" sayings**, long discourses, and the theology of the Trinity; written last, at **Ephesus**.

The Gospel of John: the theologian's Gos.front: Why is John read from Pascha to Pentecost?
The Gospel of John: the theologian's Gos.back: It is the Gospel of **eternal life already given**; the Paschal Sundays follow its stories (Thomas, the Paralytic, the Samaritan Woman, the Blind Man).

The parables and the miracles.back: "**Comparison, placing side by side**": a story from ordinary life that reveals the Kingdom to those willing to hear.

The parables and the miracles.front: The Fathers' reading of the good Samaritan
The parables and the miracles.back: The wounded man is **Adam**, the robbers **demons**, priest and Levite **the Law and prophets**, the Samaritan **Christ**, the inn **the Church**, oil and wine **the Mysteries**.
The day before Palm Sunday, keeping **the raising of Lazarus** (John 11) as a pledge of the general resurrection.

The Sermon on the Mount and the Beatitud.back: The nine "**Blessed are...**" of Matthew 5:3–12, sung as the **third antiphon** of the Liturgy.

The Sermon on the Mount and the Beatitud.front: St Gregory of Nyssa's reading of the Beatitudes
The Sermon on the Mount and the Beatitud.back: **A ladder of ascent**, from humility ("poor in spirit") to purity of heart and **the vision of God**.

The Sermon on the Mount and the Beatitud.front: Can the Sermon on the Mount be lived?
The Sermon on the Mount and the Beatitud.back: Orthodox teaching: it is neither an impossible ideal nor a law that earns salvation, but **the life of those being made like God by grace**, as the saints lived it.

The Acts of the Apostles: the Church beg.front: The four marks of the first Church's life (Acts 2:42)
The Acts of the Apostles: the Church beg.back: "The apostles' **doctrine** and **fellowship**, and in **breaking of bread**, and in **prayers**."
One of the seven deacons, **the first martyr** (Acts 7); feast **27 December**.

The Acts of the Apostles: the Church beg.front: When is Acts read in the Liturgy?
The Acts of the Apostles: the Church beg.back: **From Pascha to Pentecost**, as the Epistle, in order, beginning with Acts 1:1–8 on Pascha night.

St Paul: his life and letters.back: Born at **Tarsus**; converted **about 34–36**; three missionary journeys; martyred in Rome under Nero **about 64–67**. Feast with Peter, **29 June**.
The liturgical book of **Acts and the Epistles** read at the Liturgy.

St Paul: his life and letters.front: Why do Orthodox Christians read Paul with Chrysostom?
St Paul: his life and letters.back: **St John Chrysostom** preached homilies on **all fourteen** letters: the fullest patristic commentary on Paul.

Paul's teaching as the Church reads it:.back: "**Justification**", being made or declared righteous. In the Fathers, **real**: the start of a change, one with sanctification and theosis.

Paul's teaching as the Church reads it:.front: Paul and James on faith and works, in the Fathers' reading
Paul's teaching as the Church reads it:.back: Paul denies that **the works of the Law** save; James denies that **faith without love** is real. Both teach **"faith which worketh by love"** (Galatians 5:6).
"**Grace**": God's free gift. Salvation is wholly his gift, and freely received (synergy).

The Catholic Epistles: James, Peter, Joh.back: Seven **general letters**: James; 1–2 Peter; 1–3 John; Jude. Placed **after Acts** in Orthodox Bibles.

The Catholic Epistles: James, Peter, Joh.front: St James the Brother of the Lord
The Catholic Epistles: James, Peter, Joh.back: First **bishop of Jerusalem**; martyred **about 62**; feast **23 October**; the Liturgy of St James bears his name.

The Catholic Epistles: James, Peter, Joh.front: Which Catholic Epistle verses ground holy unction and theosis?
The Catholic Epistles: James, Peter, Joh.back: **James 5:14**: anoint the sick with oil. **2 Peter 1:4**: "**partakers of the divine nature**".

The Book of Revelation in the Orthodox C.back: "**Unveiling**": Revelation, written by John on **Patmos**, about 95.
Archbishop in Cappadocia, early 7th century: **the standard Orthodox commentary on Revelation**.
From *chílioi*, "thousand": expecting a literal **thousand-year earthly reign** (Revelation 20). Not followed by the Church; the thousand years read as **the age of the Church**.

The Fathers as interpreters of Scripture.back: Origen's Old Testament in **six parallel columns** of Hebrew and Greek: the first great work of biblical scholarship.
Archbishop of Ohrid, late 11th to early 12th century: **Gospel and Epistle commentaries distilled from Chrysostom**, still the most read.
"**Chain**": the biblical text with excerpts from many Fathers around it, verse by verse.

Scripture in the services: the lectionar.front: The Orthodox Gospel cycle through the year
Scripture in the services: the lectionar.back: **John** Pascha–Pentecost; **Matthew** from Pentecost; **Luke** from mid-September; **Mark** on Lenten weekends.
The **eleven Resurrection Gospels** read in rotation at Sunday Matins.

Scripture in the services: the lectionar.front: Where is the Old Testament read in Orthodox services?
Scripture in the services: the lectionar.back: At **Vespers on feasts** (paroimíai); in Lent **Isaiah** at the Sixth Hour, **Genesis** and **Proverbs** at Vespers; **fifteen readings** on Holy Saturday.
Greek usage: Luke begins **after the Sunday after the Elevation of the Cross**, whatever the date of Pascha.

Reading the Bible as an Orthodox Christi.front: How does the tradition teach one to read the Bible at home?
Reading the Bible as an Orthodox Christi.back: **Pray first**, read **daily** (with the lectionary), **with the Fathers**, **to obey** (James 1:22), and ask a spiritual father about hard passages.

Reading the Bible as an Orthodox Christi.front: Orthodox responses to modern biblical criticism
Reading the Bible as an Orthodox Christi.back: **Engagement** (Agourides, Stylianopoulos, Breck, Behr): use its tools as the Fathers used theirs. **Caution** (Averky): its assumptions can dissolve faith. No council has ruled.

Looking back: Scripture as the Church re.back: Status of the **readable books**; weight of the **Hebrew text**; how literally to read **Genesis 1**; the **Synoptic order**; the use of **modern criticism**.
The Bible is **the Church's book**, read in the Septuagint, in Christ, with the Fathers, in the lectionary of her worship.

Context: worship as theology.back: "**The rule of prayer is the rule of belief**" (after Prosper of Aquitaine, 5th century): doctrine is first prayed, then defined.
Greek "**work of the people**, public work": in Orthodox use, the Divine Liturgy, the Eucharist.
Isabel Florence **Hapgood**'s *Service Book of the Holy Orthodox-Catholic Apostolic (Greco-Russian) Church*: the first full English Orthodox service book.
