The temple: narthex, nave, iconostasis a.front: The three parts of an Orthodox temple
The temple: narthex, nave, iconostasis a.back: **Narthex** (porch: catechumens, candles), **nave** (the faithful), **sanctuary** (behind the iconostasis, with the Holy Table).
The **icon screen** before the sanctuary, with the **Royal Doors** (Annunciation and evangelists) and two deacons' doors. It shows heaven, not hides it.
The table on the **north side** of the sanctuary where the bread and wine are prepared.
"**Ruler of all**": the image of Christ in the dome.

Icons: the theology of the image.front: Why can God be painted, in Orthodox teaching?
Icons: the theology of the image.back: Because **in Christ the invisible God became visible**. To refuse his icon would deny the Incarnation (St John of Damascus).
The Seventh Ecumenical Council: icons are venerated, for **"the honour which is paid to the image passes on to that which the image represents"**.
The final restoration of icons under **Empress Theodora**; kept on the **first Sunday of Great Lent**.
About **675–749**: defender of icons: "I do not worship matter, I worship the God of matter, who became matter for my sake".

Clergy, servers and vestments.back: The priest's **stole**, round the neck and falling in front: **no Mystery is served without it**.
The bishop's broad stole: **the lost sheep carried by the Good Shepherd**.
The priest's large **cape**, worn over the other vestments at the Liturgy.

Clergy, servers and vestments.front: Who may be married among Orthodox clergy?
Clergy, servers and vestments.back: **Deacons and priests**, if married **before ordination to the diaconate**. **Bishops** are celibate, chosen from monastics.

The three Liturgies: Chrysostom, Basil a.front: When is the Liturgy of St Basil served?
The three Liturgies: Chrysostom, Basil a.back: **Ten times a year**: Lent Sundays 1–5, Holy Thursday, Holy Saturday, the eves (or days) of the Nativity and Theophany, and **1 January**.
Vespers with Communion from Gifts consecrated the Sunday before: **Lenten Wednesdays and Fridays** and the first three days of Holy Week. Attributed to **St Gregory the Dialogist**.
Archbishop of Constantinople **398–404**, died **407**; the everyday Liturgy bears his name.

The three Liturgies: Chrysostom, Basil a.front: The three parts of the Divine Liturgy
The three Liturgies: Chrysostom, Basil a.back: **Proskomedia** (preparation), **Liturgy of the Catechumens** (the Word), **Liturgy of the Faithful** (the Eucharist).

The Divine Liturgy 1: the Proskomedia.back: The **leavened loaf** for the Eucharist, stamped **IC XC NIKA**, "Jesus Christ conquers".
The **central square cut from the prosphora** at the Proskomedia, which becomes the Body of Christ.

The Divine Liturgy 1: the Proskomedia.front: What is placed on the diskos at the Proskomedia?
The Divine Liturgy 1: the Proskomedia.back: The **Lamb**; the **Theotokos** on its right; **nine ranks of saints** on its left; below, **the living** and **the departed**: the whole Church.
"**Instead of the gift**": the blessed bread from the prosphora, given out at the end of the Liturgy.

The Divine Liturgy 2: \"Blessed is the k.front: The first words of the Divine Liturgy
The Divine Liturgy 2: \"Blessed is the k.back: "**Blessed is the kingdom of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit**, now, and ever, and unto ages of ages."
The deacon's petitions opening the service, beginning "**In peace let us pray to the Lord**", answered by "Lord, have mercy".

The Divine Liturgy 2: \"Blessed is the k.front: The three parts of every Orthodox litany
The Divine Liturgy 2: \"Blessed is the k.back: **Deacon's petitions**, the **people's response**, and the **priest's exclamation** (*ekphṓnēsis*), a doxology to the Trinity.

The Divine Liturgy 3: the antiphons and.back: Sung after the second antiphon; attributed to **Emperor Justinian I** (527–565). A Christology in one breath: incarnate "without change of essence", "one of the Holy Trinity".
The procession with the **Gospel book**; once the real entry of clergy and people into the church.
"Wisdom! Upright!" (Hapgood: "**Wisdom, O believers!**"): the call before the entrance and the readings.

The Divine Liturgy 4: the Trisagion, the.back: "**Thrice-holy**": "O Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal One, have mercy upon us." Sung at **Chalcedon (451)**.
"**That which is set before**": the psalm verse before the Epistle.

The Divine Liturgy 4: the Trisagion, the.front: When is the Trisagion replaced by "As many as have been baptized into Christ"?
The Divine Liturgy 4: the Trisagion, the.back: On the old **baptismal days**: Nativity, Theophany, Lazarus Saturday, Holy Saturday, Pascha and Bright Week, Pentecost.

The Divine Liturgy 5: the catechumens an.back: Sung at the Great Entrance, introduced in the **570s** under Justin II: "Let us, the Cherubim mystically representing... all cares terrestrial now lay aside."
The procession carrying the **diskos and chalice** to the altar during the Cherubic Hymn. The gifts are **not yet consecrated**.

The Divine Liturgy 5: the catechumens an.front: Why are the catechumens still dismissed at the Liturgy?
The Divine Liturgy 5: the catechumens an.back: Of old only the baptised stayed for the Eucharist; the words remain to mark **the start of the Liturgy of the Faithful**.

The Divine Liturgy 6: the kiss of peace.front: "Let us love one another, that with one accord we may confess..."
The Divine Liturgy 6: the kiss of peace.back: The people complete it: "**Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the Trinity, one in Essence and undivided.**" Love leads to confessing the Trinity.
Once an order to **close the church doors** before the Mystery; now, the doors of the heart.

The Divine Liturgy 6: the kiss of peace.front: "A mercy of peace, a sacrifice of praise": what it means
The Divine Liturgy 6: the kiss of peace.back: The people's answer before the anaphora: the Eucharist is **God's mercy bringing peace**, and the Church's **offering of thanksgiving** (Hebrews 13:15).

Reading: the anaphora of St John Chrysos.back: "**Lifting up, offering**": the eucharistic prayer, from "Lift up your hearts" to the epiclesis.
"**Remembrance**": the anaphora's recalling of the Cross, Grave, Resurrection, Ascension, Sitting, and even **the Second Coming**.
"...we offer unto thee, in behalf of all, and for all": the gifts are **God's creation given back**.

Reading: the anaphora of St John Chrysos.front: The parts of the anaphora of St John Chrysostom, in order

The Divine Liturgy 7: the epiclesis and.back: "**Invocation**": the prayer that the Father send the Spirit on the people and the Gifts. Orthodox teaching places the consecration here.

The Divine Liturgy 7: the epiclesis and.front: The priest's words at the blessing of the Gifts (Hapgood)
The Divine Liturgy 7: the epiclesis and.back: "**And make this bread the precious Body of thy Christ.**" "And make that which is in this chalice the precious Blood of thy Christ." "**Transmuting them by thy Holy Spirit.**"

The Divine Liturgy 7: the epiclesis and.front: Axion estin ("Meet is it, in truth")
The Divine Liturgy 7: the epiclesis and.back: Hymn to the Theotokos after the consecration; first part by Athonite tradition from the Archangel Gabriel (10th century), second ("More honourable than the Cherubim") by **St Cosmas** (8th century).

The Divine Liturgy 8: the Lord's Prayer,.front: "Holy things unto the Holy" and its answer
The Divine Liturgy 8: the Lord's Prayer,.back: The people reply: "**One only is holy, one only is the Lord, Jesus Christ**, in the glory of God the Father." Holiness is Christ's, given to those he sanctifies.
"**Boiling**": hot water added to the chalice before Communion: "**The warmth of faith, full of the Holy Spirit**".
The **spoon** with which the Body and Blood are given together from the chalice.

The Divine Liturgy 9: thanksgiving and d.back: Sung after Communion: "we have received the heavenly Spirit; we have found the true faith"; the **Pentecost** hymn of Vespers.
Read by the priest **among the people** at the end of the Liturgy: "O Lord, who blessest those who bless thee..."
Phrase of Orthodox missiologists (**Ion Bria**, **Archbishop Anastasios**) for the life of service that follows the Eucharist.

Preparing for Communion: fasting, confes.back: **No food or drink from midnight** (or the evening before) until Communion; the sick and infants excused.
18th-century Athonite movement; **St Nikodemos** and **St Makarios of Corinth** urged **frequent Communion**.

Preparing for Communion: fasting, confes.front: Confession before every Communion? The two Orthodox practices
Preparing for Communion: fasting, confes.back: **Russian and much Slavic** practice: yes, as a norm. **Greek, Antiochian, Romanian** and much diaspora practice: regular confession, not necessarily each time. The spiritual father guides.

The daily cycle of services: from Vesper.front: Why does the Orthodox liturgical day begin at sunset?
The daily cycle of services: from Vesper.back: Following **Genesis** and Jewish reckoning: "the evening and the morning were the first day". **Every feast begins with Vespers the evening before.**

The daily cycle of services: from Vesper.front: The daily cycle of services, in order
The daily cycle of services: from Vesper.back: **Vespers, Compline, Midnight Office, Matins, First Hour, Third, Sixth, Ninth**, and the Liturgy.
**Vespers, Matins and the First Hour** joined on the eves of Sundays and feasts.

Vespers and Matins: the evening and morn.back: The **lamp-lighting hymn** of Vespers, one of the oldest Christian hymns; already "the ancient form" for **St Basil** (*On the Holy Spirit* 29.73, 375).
**Psalm 103** (creation), litany (the fall), "**Lord, I have cried**" with incense, the entrance (Christ's coming), **O Gladsome Light**, readings, **Song of Simeon**.
The **nine-ode hymn** of Matins, modelled on the biblical odes; developed by **Andrew of Crete, John of Damascus and Cosmas** (7th–8th centuries).
**Six Psalms** in darkness, "God is the Lord", the **Resurrection Gospel** from the altar, the **canon**, the Magnificat, the Praises, the **Great Doxology** at dawn.

The Typikon and the service books.back: The **book of rules** that orders each day's services. Today the **Jerusalem (Sabaite) Typikon**, with Violakis's parish Typikon (1888) in Greek use.
"Of the month": **twelve volumes** with the hymns of the saints and fixed feasts.

The Typikon and the service books.front: Triodion and Pentecostarion: what each covers
The Typikon and the service books.back: **Triodion**: the pre-Lenten weeks, Lent and Holy Week. **Pentecostarion**: Pascha to All Saints.
The **priest's book**: Liturgies, Mysteries, blessings (Slavonic *Sluzhebnik* and *Trebnik*).

The weekly cycle: the days of the week a.front: The themes of the Orthodox week
The weekly cycle: the days of the week a.back: **Sun** Resurrection; **Mon** angels; **Tue** the Forerunner; **Wed** Cross and Theotokos (fast); **Thu** apostles and St Nicholas; **Fri** Cross (fast); **Sat** all saints and the departed.
"**Eight tones**": the book of weekly hymns in eight modes, one tone a week; attributed to **St John of Damascus**.

The weekly cycle: the days of the week a.front: Didache on Wednesday and Friday fasting
The weekly cycle: the days of the week a.back: Late 1st or early 2nd century: fast "on the **fourth day** and the **Preparation (Friday)**", not with the hypocrites.

The yearly cycle: the fixed and movable.back: The **beginning of the Orthodox Church year**. First great feast: the Nativity of the Theotokos (8 Sept); last: the Dormition (15 Aug).
**Nicaea (325)**: one Sunday for all. First Sunday after the first full moon after the equinox, by the **Julian Paschalion**; this century it falls **4 April–8 May**.
Adopted at a congress under **Meletios IV**; matches the Gregorian for fixed feasts until 2800. Pascha still kept by the Julian Paschalion.

The twelve great feasts: the feasts of t.front: The eight great feasts of the Lord, with dates
The twelve great feasts: the feasts of t.back: **Elevation of the Cross** 14 Sept; **Nativity** 25 Dec; **Theophany** 6 Jan; **Meeting** 2 Feb; **Palm Sunday**; **Ascension** (40th day); **Pentecost** (50th day); **Transfiguration** 6 Aug.
"**Appearance of God**": the **baptism of Christ** and the revelation of the Trinity; the **Great Blessing of Waters**.
"**Giving back**": the leave-taking, last day of a feast's afterfeast.

The twelve great feasts: the feasts of t.front: The four great feasts of the Theotokos, with dates
The twelve great feasts: the feasts of t.back: **Nativity** 8 Sept; **Entry into the Temple** 21 Nov; **Annunciation** 25 Mar; **Dormition** 15 Aug.
**15 August**: her falling asleep and being taken, body and soul, into heaven; preceded by a **two-week fast**.
2nd-century account of the Theotokos's childhood, not Scripture, source of the feasts of her **Nativity** and **Entry**.

The twelve great feasts: the feasts of t.front: Is Pascha one of the twelve great feasts?
The twelve great feasts: the feasts of t.back: **No: it stands above them**, the feast of feasts, with a forty-day season.

Great Lent: from the Triodion to Holy We.front: The five Sundays before Great Lent
The five Sundays of Great Lent
Great Lent: from the Triodion to Holy We.back: **1** Triumph of Orthodoxy; **2** St Gregory Palamas; **3** the Cross; **4** St John Climacus; **5** St Mary of Egypt.

Great Lent: from the Triodion to Holy We.front: Great Canon of St Andrew of Crete
Great Lent: from the Triodion to Holy We.back: Andrew, about **660–740**: the longest canon; read on the **first four evenings of Lent** and in full on **Thursday of the fifth week**.

Great Lent: from the Triodion to Holy We.front: Prayer of St Ephrem the Syrian
Great Lent: from the Triodion to Holy We.back: Lenten prayer with prostrations: "O Lord and Master of my life...", ending "**grant that I may perceive my own transgressions, and judge not my brother**".

Holy Week and Pascha.back: Served on the first evenings of Holy Week, built on Matthew 25:6, with the icon of **Christ the Bridegroom**.
The cloth embroidered with **the dead Christ**, laid in a flower-decked tomb on Great Friday and carried in procession.

Holy Week and Pascha.front: The services of Holy Thursday to Holy Saturday
Holy Week and Pascha.back: **Thu**: Basil Liturgy (Mystical Supper); **Thu evening**: Twelve Passion Gospels; **Fri**: Royal Hours, Vespers with the epitaphios, Lamentations; **Sat**: Vesperal Basil Liturgy with **fifteen readings**.
The week after Pascha, kept **as one day**: Royal Doors open, no fasting, the **Artos** before the iconostasis.

The fasts and the rule of fasting.front: The four Orthodox fasting seasons, with dates
The fasts and the rule of fasting.back: **Nativity** 15 Nov–24 Dec; **Great Lent and Holy Week**; **Apostles'** from Monday after All Saints to 28 June; **Dormition** 1–14 Aug.
No **meat, dairy, eggs, fish**; no **wine or olive oil** on weekdays of the strict fasts. Applied **with economy** by the spiritual father.

The fasts and the rule of fasting.front: The single fast days of the Orthodox year
The fasts and the rule of fasting.back: Every **Wednesday and Friday**; the **Elevation of the Cross** (14 Sept); the **Beheading of the Forerunner** (29 Aug); the **Eve of Theophany** (5 Jan).

Confession: the Mystery of repentance.back: "**Repentance**", literally a change of mind: turning the whole person back to God.

Confession: the Mystery of repentance.front: In confession, who hears and who is the priest?
Confession: the Mystery of repentance.back: **Christ hears**; the priest is "**but a witness**", and confession is coming "**to the physician**" (Hapgood's rite).
A **penance**, given as **medicine**, not payment: prayers, prostrations, almsgiving or abstaining from Communion for a time.
**Spiritual father**, confessor (Russian *dukhovnik*); in Greek practice a priest specially blessed to hear confessions.

Marriage: the crowning.front: The two parts of the Orthodox marriage service
Marriage: the crowning.back: **Betrothal** (rings, candles) and **Crowning** (crowns, Epistle and Gospel of Cana, **common cup**, **dance of Isaiah**).

Marriage: the crowning.front: What do the marriage crowns mean?
Marriage: the crowning.back: **Royalty** (the household as a little Church), **martyrdom** (self-giving), and **the Kingdom** to come.

Marriage: the crowning.front: Second marriage in the Orthodox Church
Marriage: the crowning.back: One marriage is the norm; a **second and at most third** may be blessed **by economy**, with a **penitential rite**.

Holy unction and ordination.back: "**Prayer-oil**": **seven Epistles, seven Gospels, seven anointings**, ideally seven priests; for any sickness of soul or body; **general unction on Holy Wednesday**.
"**Laying on of hands**": ordination of deacon, priest and bishop. Minor orders by *cheirothesía*.

Holy unction and ordination.front: When in the Liturgy is each order ordained?
Holy unction and ordination.back: **Bishop**: after the Trisagion; **priest**: after the Great Entrance; **deacon**: after the anaphora.
"**He is worthy!**": the acclamation of clergy and people at an ordination.

Looking back: worship.back: **Frequency of Communion** and confession before it; women's Communion during menstruation; **the calendar**; the Third Hour troparion in the anaphora; **deaconesses**.
**The Spirit makes the Church, the Church reads the Scripture he inspired, and the Church prays**: at the centre is the Liturgy.

Context: from Pentecost to Chalcedon.back: From *oikouménē*, "the inhabited world": a council of bishops whose teaching **the whole Church afterwards receives**. The Orthodox Church counts **seven**.

Context: from Pentecost to Chalcedon.front: The first four ecumenical councils, with dates
Why did the early councils define doctrine at all?
Context: from Pentecost to Chalcedon.back: To answer a teaching that had been put forward: **the Church defined only what had been denied**, and as little as she needed.

The apostolic age: from Jerusalem to the.back: The descent of the Holy Spirit on the apostles in Jerusalem, fifty days after Pascha (Acts 2): **the birthday of the Church**.
The first church of Jews and Gentiles together, where the disciples were **first called Christians** (Acts 11:26).
Title of saints who spread the faith as the apostles did: e.g. **Constantine and Helen**, **Cyril and Methodius**, **Mary Magdalene**.

The Council of Jerusalem: the first coun.back: Acts 15: Gentile converts **need not be circumcised or keep the Law of Moses**; James gave the judgement.

The Council of Jerusalem: the first coun.front: Why is "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us" the charter of the councils?
The Council of Jerusalem: the first coun.back: The bishops **do not vote a doctrine into being**: they meet, hear Scripture and testimony, and **recognise together what the Spirit says**.
Slavonic, from *sobor*, "council, gathering": **conciliarity**, the Church deciding together rather than by one voice alone.

The Apostolic Fathers: Clement, Ignatius.back: "Teaching of the Twelve Apostles", late 1st or early 2nd century: church manual with the **Two Ways**, baptism, the **Wednesday and Friday fast**, the Eucharist.

The Apostolic Fathers: Clement, Ignatius.front: St Clement of Rome, Letter to the Corinthians (about 96)
The Apostolic Fathers: Clement, Ignatius.back: Rome writes to Corinth, which had deposed its presbyters: **the first written statement of apostolic succession**. Feast 25 November.
**Bishop** (*epískopos*, overseer), **presbyter** (*presbýteros*, elder), **deacon** (*diákonos*, servant): in place by Ignatius's day, about 107.

Reading: St Ignatius of Antioch to the S.back: Bishop of Antioch, *Theophóros*; wrote **seven letters** on the way to martyrdom in Rome under Trajan. Feast **20 December**.
From *dokéō*, "to seem": the teaching that **Christ only seemed to have a body** and to suffer. Ignatius answers it with "truly".

Reading: St Ignatius of Antioch to the S.front: Why does Ignatius tie Christ's flesh, the Eucharist and the bishop together?
Reading: St Ignatius of Antioch to the S.back: If Christ's flesh is real, **the Eucharist is his real flesh**; and the church gathered round **one bishop and one altar** is where Christ is.
"According to the whole": complete, lacking nothing. **First surviving use of "the Catholic Church"**: Ignatius, *Smyrnaeans* 8.

The martyrs: from St Stephen to St Polyc.back: Greek: **witness**, as in court. A martyr's death **bears witness to Christ**; the day of death is kept as the **birthday** into heaven.
Bishop, disciple of St John by Irenaeus's account; burned at Smyrna. His church kept his bones and his day: **earliest witness to relics and saints' feasts**. Feast **23 February**.

The martyrs: from St Stephen to St Polyc.front: Why did Rome put Christians to death?
The martyrs: from St Stephen to St Polyc.back: Not usually for believing in Christ, but for **refusing to honour the gods and the emperor**, seen as atheism and disloyalty.

The great persecutions: Decius, Valerian.back: Everyone had to **sacrifice and obtain a certificate** (*libellus*). Raised the question of the **lapsed**.
Under **Diocletian** and Galerius: churches destroyed, Scriptures burned, all ordered to sacrifice. Era of **St George**, **St Demetrios**, **St Panteleimon**.
One who **suffered for Christ under persecution and survived**.

St Justin Martyr and the apologists.back: Philosopher-convert, taught in Rome; *First Apology* (about 155) and *Dialogue with Trypho*; beheaded about 165. Feast **1 June**.
"Seed-bearing Word": Justin's teaching that **all share in the Word**, so the philosophers held seeds of the truth that Christians have whole in Christ.

St Justin Martyr and the apologists.front: What does Justin's First Apology 65 to 67 show about early worship?
St Justin Martyr and the apologists.back: The **Sunday Eucharist** already in its Liturgy shape: readings, sermon, prayers, kiss of peace, offering, thanksgiving, **Amen**, communion, alms.

Gnosticism and St Irenaeus of Lyons.back: From *gnōsis*, "knowledge": 2nd-century schools teaching **matter is evil, made by a lesser god**, salvation is escape by **secret knowledge**.

Gnosticism and St Irenaeus of Lyons.front: St Irenaeus of Lyons (about 130 to about 202)
Gnosticism and St Irenaeus of Lyons.back: Heard Polycarp as a boy; bishop of Lyons; ***Against Heresies*** (about 180). Feast **23 August**.
"Summing up again": Irenaeus's teaching that **Christ the new Adam retraces human life and undoes the fall by obedience**.

The rule of faith, the canon and the bis.back: *Kanṓn tēs alētheías*: the **baptismal summary of the faith** (one God the Creator, Christ, the Spirit), the key for reading Scripture.
Rejected the **Old Testament** and kept only an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul; pushed the Church to name her canon.
The **first list of exactly the 27 books** of the New Testament.

Alexandria's school: St Clement and Orig.back: Alexandrian scholar: the **Hexapla**, commentaries, *On First Principles*. Tortured under Decius. Teachings later condemned in the **sixth century**.
"Restoration": the **universal restoration** of all rational beings, speculated by Origen and rejected by the councils of the sixth century.

Alexandria's school: St Clement and Orig.front: How does the Orthodox Church receive Origen?
Alexandria's school: St Clement and Orig.back: As **a teacher the Fathers read, used and corrected**: his spiritual reading of Scripture passed into the Church, his speculative system did not.

St Cyprian of Carthage, the lapsed and t.back: Bishop; *On the Unity of the Catholic Church* (251); beheaded **14 September 258**. Orthodox feast **31 August**.
"Household management": the bishop's power to **apply a canon with mercy** for a person's salvation.

St Cyprian of Carthage, the lapsed and t.front: How did Cyprian answer the question of the lapsed?
St Cyprian of Carthage, the lapsed and t.back: Not at once and not never: **readmission after a period of penance**, graded by the fall, under the bishop.

St Constantine and the end of persecutio.front: Battle of the Milvian Bridge (28 October 312)
St Constantine and the end of persecutio.back: Constantine defeats Maxentius under **the sign of Christ**.
Agreement of Constantine and Licinius: **freedom of worship** and return of Christians' property.
Equal-to-the-Apostles, feast **21 May**. Helen by tradition found the **True Cross** in Jerusalem about 326.
Constantine's **New Rome** on the site of Byzantium.

Arius and the crisis at Alexandria.back: Presbyter of Alexandria who taught **the Son is a creature, made out of nothing**: "there was when he was not".

Arius and the crisis at Alexandria.front: Why could the Church not accept Arius's teaching?
Arius and the crisis at Alexandria.back: **Only God can save**: a created Son cannot unite us to God; worship of Christ would be idolatry; baptism is into God's name.
Bishop about **312 to 328**; first condemned Arius, about 318 to 320; attended Nicaea with his deacon **Athanasius**.

The First Ecumenical Council: Nicaea (32.back: Summoned by Constantine; the **318 Fathers**. Confessed the Son **homooúsios** with the Father; fixed a common **Pascha**; 20 canons.
"Of one essence", consubstantial (*homós* same, *ousía* essence): **whatever the Father is as God, the Son is**.
Begetting is not creating: **a father begets his own kind**; so the Son is God from God, not a creature.

The First Ecumenical Council: Nicaea (32.front: Sunday of the Fathers of the First Council
The First Ecumenical Council: Nicaea (32.back: The **seventh Sunday of Pascha**, after the Ascension.

St Athanasius and the fifty years after.back: Bishop of Alexandria **328 to 373**, **exiled five times**; *On the Incarnation*, *Life of Antony*. Feasts **18 January** and **2 May**.
**Homoian**: the Son simply "like" the Father (*hómoios*). **Homoiousian**: "of like essence" (*homoioúsios*). Both rivals to *homooúsios*.
Athanasius's synod that **welcomed those who meant the same faith in other words**, beginning the reconciliation.

The Cappadocians and the divinity of the.back: **Basil the Great**, **Gregory the Theologian**, **John Chrysostom**, honoured together.
"Spirit-fighters", also called **Macedonians**: accepted the Son's divinity but held the **Holy Spirit a creature**.

The Cappadocians and the divinity of the.front: How did St Basil argue for the Spirit's divinity in On the Holy Spirit?
The Cappadocians and the divinity of the.back: From **worship**: the Church glorifies the Spirit with the Father and Son; and he does **what only God does**, sanctifying and giving life.
Sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa; her ascetic household formed them. Feast **19 July**.

The Second Ecumenical Council: Constanti.back: Summoned by **Theodosius I**; about 150 bishops; confessed the **Holy Spirit as Lord and Giver of Life**; condemned Pneumatomachi and Apollinarians; the Creed completed.
Teaching of Apollinarius of Laodicea that **the Word took a human body without a human mind**. Condemned in 381.

The Second Ecumenical Council: Constanti.front: Why does the Creed of 381 not call the Spirit homooúsios?
The Second Ecumenical Council: Constanti.back: Following Basil's tact: it confesses his Godhead by **equal worship** ("worshipped and glorified") and the divine title **Lord**.

The canons of the first councils: Pascha.back: Constantinople has the **prerogative of honour after Rome**, "because Constantinople is New Rome".
Five patriarchates in order: **Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem**.
"Rudder": the Orthodox collection of the **canons with commentary** by St Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain.

Nestorius and St Cyril: the Theotokos qu.back: "The one who gave birth to God": Mary's title, because **her Son is God the Word**. Defended at Ephesus, 431.
Archbishop of Constantinople from **428**; preferred **Christotokos**; seen as dividing Christ into **two sons**.
Bishop **412 to 444**; Third Letter to Nestorius with **twelve anathemas** (430). Feasts **9 June** and **18 January**.

Nestorius and St Cyril: the Theotokos qu.front: Why is the title Theotokos a teaching about Christ?
Nestorius and St Cyril: the Theotokos qu.back: It says **who her Son is**: the child she bore is God the Word made flesh.

The Third Ecumenical Council: Ephesus (4.back: Opened by Cyril **22 June 431**; deposed **Nestorius**; confessed Mary **Theotokos**; Canon 7 against a different creed; Canon 8 on Cyprus.
Agreement of Cyril and John of Antioch: **perfect God and perfect man**, consubstantial with the Father and with us, a **union of two natures**, Mary Theotokos.

The Third Ecumenical Council: Ephesus (4.front: The Assyrian Church of the East
The Third Ecumenical Council: Ephesus (4.back: The church of the Persian Empire that **did not receive Ephesus**; spread to India and China. "Nestorian" is others' name for it.

Eutyches, the Robber Council (449) and t.back: Archimandrite in Constantinople: **two natures before the union, one after**; would not call Christ's body consubstantial with ours. Condemned by St Flavian, **448**.
Pope Leo's letter to Flavian: **one person; each nature keeps its properties** and acts in communion with the other.
Under **Dioscorus**: restored Eutyches, deposed Flavian. Leo called it a ***latrocinium***, "robber council".

The Fourth Ecumenical Council: Chalcedon.back: Summoned by **Marcian and Pulcheria**; one Christ **in two natures**; Canon 28 on Constantinople; Jerusalem made a patriarchate.
***asynchýtōs*** without confusion, ***atréptōs*** without change, ***adiairétōs*** without division, ***achōrístōs*** without separation.

The Fourth Ecumenical Council: Chalcedon.front: What does Chalcedon confess about Christ?
The Fourth Ecumenical Council: Chalcedon.back: **One person (*hypóstasis*), the eternal Word, in two natures**, Godhead and manhood, each keeping its own properties.

The Fourth Ecumenical Council: Chalcedon.front: Sunday of the Fathers of the Fourth Council

Why some churches did not receive Chalce.back: From *mía phýsis*, "one nature": the Oriental Orthodox term, after Cyril's **"one incarnate nature of God the Word"**. They reject "Monophysite".

Why some churches did not receive Chalce.front: Why did the miaphysites object to "in two natures"?
Why some churches did not receive Chalce.back: It sounded to them like **Nestorius**, dividing Christ; they held to **Cyril's "one nature"** in the sense of one concrete Christ, and preferred "**from** two natures".
Patriarch of Antioch **512 to 518**; the great theologian of the miaphysite position, honoured as a saint by the Oriental Orthodox.

The Oriental Orthodox churches.back: **Coptic**, **Syriac**, **Armenian**, **Ethiopian**, **Eritrean** and **Malankara** churches, in communion with each other; did not receive Chalcedon.
Emperor Zeno's "act of union", setting Chalcedon aside; satisfied neither side and led to the **Acacian schism** (484 to 519).
Ge'ez: **"made one"**, in the name of the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches.

Looking back: the faith of the four coun.front: What links the doctrine of the four councils to salvation?
Looking back: the faith of the four coun.back: Each protected **theosis**: a creature cannot deify, nor a created Spirit sanctify; two sons cannot unite God and man; a manhood swallowed is not ours healed.

Looking back: the faith of the four coun.front: What made a council ecumenical in the early Church?
Looking back: the faith of the four coun.back: Not numbers or imperial summons but **reception by the whole Church**: 449 was overturned, 381 received though Eastern.

Context: from Chalcedon to the fall of C.back: "Romans": what the people of the "Byzantine" Empire called themselves. **"Byzantine" is a 16th-century Western label.**

Context: from Chalcedon to the fall of C.front: The last three ecumenical councils, with dates
What do the Fifth, Sixth and Seventh Councils have in common?
Context: from Chalcedon to the fall of C.back: All are **about Christ**, drawing out Chalcedon: **one of the Trinity suffered**; **two wills**; **he can be portrayed**.

Justinian, Hagia Sophia and the ideal of.back: Emperor; *Corpus Iuris Civilis*; built **Hagia Sophia**; summoned the **Fifth Council (553)**. Commemorated **14 November**.
Church of the **Holy Wisdom** in Constantinople, by Anthemius and Isidore; cathedral of the Ecumenical Patriarch for nine centuries.
"Harmony": the Byzantine ideal of **priesthood and empire as two gifts of God** serving one Christian people (Justinian, *Novel 6*, 535).

The Fifth Ecumenical Council: Constantin.back: Under Justinian and Patriarch Eutychius: condemned the **Three Chapters**; confessed that **one of the Holy Trinity suffered in the flesh**.
**Theodore of Mopsuestia** (person and writings), **Theodoret's** writings against Cyril, and **Ibas's** letter to Mari.
"**One of the Trinity suffered in the flesh**": the one who suffered is God the Word, though not in his divine nature.

Monoenergism and Monothelitism: one will.back: From *hén thélēma*, "one will": that **Christ has only one will**. Taught in the **Ecthesis (638)**; condemned in **681**.
"One activity": Christ has two natures but **one divine-human activity**. Patriarch **Sergius**, 610s to 630s.

Monoenergism and Monothelitism: one will.front: Why could the Church not confess only one will in Christ?
Monoenergism and Monothelitism: one will.back: **Will belongs to nature**: without a human will Christ is not fully man, and **what is not assumed is not healed**, so our fallen will would not be saved.
Edict of **Constans II** forbidding all discussion of one or two wills: **silence by decree**.

St Maximus the Confessor and the two wil.back: Monk and theologian of the **two wills**; disputed with Pyrrhus (645); mutilated and exiled. Feast **21 January**.

St Maximus the Confessor and the two wil.front: Thélēma physikón and gnṓmē (in St Maximus)
St Maximus the Confessor and the two wil.back: **Natural will**: the power to will proper to human nature, which Christ has. **Gnomic will**: hesitating, deliberating choice, which he has not.

St Maximus the Confessor and the two wil.front: How does St Maximus read Gethsemane?
St Maximus the Confessor and the two wil.back: Christ's human will shrinks from death as nature does, then **freely embraces the Father's will**: there our will is turned back to God.

The Lateran Synod (649) and the sufferin.back: Pope **Martin I's** synod in Rome, with Maximus's help: confessed **two wills and two activities**; condemned the Ecthesis and Typos.

The Lateran Synod (649) and the sufferin.front: St Martin the Confessor, Pope of Rome
The Lateran Synod (649) and the sufferin.back: Arrested 653, exiled to **Cherson**, died **655**. Orthodox feast **14 April**.

The Lateran Synod (649) and the sufferin.front: Why did St Maximus refuse to submit even when the patriarchs had?
The Lateran Synod (649) and the sufferin.back: He held that **the faith does not depend on numbers**: the Church is wherever the right confession is.

The Sixth Ecumenical Council: Constantin.front: Sixth Ecumenical Council, Constantinople III (680 to 681)
The Sixth Ecumenical Council: Constantin.back: Under **Constantine IV**, with Pope Agatho's letter: **two natural wills and two natural operations**, the human will following, not resisting.

The Sixth Ecumenical Council: Constantin.front: What does the Sixth Council teach about Christ's human will and theosis?
The Sixth Ecumenical Council: Constantin.back: It is **"not contrary to God but altogether deified"**: deified yet not suppressed, but preserved. The pattern for every Christian.

The Sixth Ecumenical Council: Constantin.front: Pope Honorius and the Sixth Council
The Sixth Ecumenical Council: Constantin.back: Honorius of Rome (625 to 638) was **anathematized by name** for writing of one will in Christ.

The Council in Trullo (692) and the cano.back: "Fifth-Sixth": **102 canons** completing the Fifth and Sixth Councils; Orthodox treat them with the Sixth Council's authority.
Christ to be depicted **in human form, not as a lamb**, to recall his life in the flesh.
Married men may be ordained and **keep their wives**.

The rise of Islam and the Orthodox patri.back: From Syriac *malkā*, "king": the **Chalcedonian Christians** of the Middle East, the "king's men"; Arabic-speaking by the 9th century.
"Protected people": Christians and Jews under Muslim rule, allowed worship in return for the **jizya** tax and under restrictions.

The rise of Islam and the Orthodox patri.front: Fall of Jerusalem to the Arabs (637 or 638)
The rise of Islam and the Orthodox patri.back: Surrendered by **St Sophronius** to the Caliph **Umar**.

The first Iconoclasm: Leo III, Constanti.back: From *eikṓn* "image" and *kláō* "break": the **destruction and rejection of holy images**, 726/730 to 787 and 815 to 843.
Constantine V's iconoclast council of **338 bishops, no patriarchs**; anathematized Germanos and John of Damascus. Rejected by the Church.

The first Iconoclasm: Leo III, Constanti.front: Why is defending the icon a defence of the Incarnation?
The first Iconoclasm: Leo III, Constanti.back: If Christ cannot be portrayed, he did not truly become **visible, touchable flesh**. The icon shows **the person of the Word made man**.
Patriarch **715 to 730**; resigned rather than sign Leo III's edict against images. Feast **12 May**.

St John of Damascus and the defence of t.front: St John of Damascus (about 675 to about 749)
St John of Damascus and the defence of t.back: Monk of **St Sabbas**; three treatises **on the holy images**; *Exact Exposition*; Paschal Canon. Feast **4 December**.

St John of Damascus and the defence of t.front: How does St John of Damascus distinguish latreía from proskýnēsis?
St John of Damascus and the defence of t.back: ***Latreía*** (worship) is for **God alone**; ***proskýnēsis*** (veneration by bowing or kissing) honours icons, the Cross, holy people, and passes to God.

St John of Damascus and the defence of t.front: What changed with the Incarnation, for St John of Damascus?
St John of Damascus and the defence of t.back: The invisible God could not be depicted; **now God has been seen in the flesh**, so what is visible of him may be painted.

The Seventh Ecumenical Council: Nicaea I.back: Under Empress **Irene** and Patriarch **Tarasios**, with Hadrian I's legates: **restored the holy icons**; 22 canons (relics in every altar).

The Seventh Ecumenical Council: Nicaea I.front: Sunday of the Fathers of the Seventh Council

The Seventh Ecumenical Council: Nicaea I.back: Frankish council that **rejected Nicaea II**, working from a poor Latin translation; see the *Libri Carolini*.

Reading: the definition of the Seventh E.back: "**Honourable reverence**": the honour given to icons by Nicaea II, distinct from *latreía*, the worship of God.

Reading: the definition of the Seventh E.front: Why, according to Nicaea II, are icons made at all?
Reading: the definition of the Seventh E.back: So that **the Incarnation is shown as real**, "not merely phantastic", and the faithful are **lifted to the memory of their prototypes, and to a longing after them**.

Reading: the definition of the Seventh E.front: Where does the honour given to an icon go?
Reading: the definition of the Seventh E.back: "**The honour which is paid to the image passes on to that which the image represents**" (Nicaea II, after St Basil).

The second Iconoclasm and St Theodore th.back: Abbot of **Stoudios**; monastic reformer, hymnographer, defender of icons; exiled three times. Feast **11 November**.

The second Iconoclasm and St Theodore th.front: What does St Theodore the Studite say an icon depicts?
The second Iconoclasm and St Theodore th.back: **The hypostasis, not the nature**: Christ's icon shows the **person of the Word** in the human features he truly has.
"**Circumscribed**": Christ, being truly man, has a particular body and place, so **he can be depicted**.

The Triumph of Orthodoxy (843) and the S.back: Restoration of the icons under **Empress Theodora** and Patriarch **Methodios**; kept on the **first Sunday of Great Lent**.
Document read on the Sunday of Orthodoxy: **acclamations ("Eternal memory!") and anathemas**; later additions include Palamas's teaching.
*Orthós* "right" + *dóxa* "belief, glory": **right belief and right glory**. Slavonic *Pravoslávie*, "right glorifying".
*Anáthema*, "set apart": a declaration that a teaching or its holder is **outside the Church's communion**.

St Photios the Great.front: St Photios the Great (about 810 to about 893)
St Photios the Great.back: Patriarch of Constantinople **858 to 867** and **877 to 886**; *Bibliotheca*; *Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit*. Feast **6 February**.
With Pope John VIII's legates: **restored Photios**, annulled 869 to 870, **confirmed the Creed without addition**. Some Orthodox call it the **Eighth Ecumenical**.
**St Photios the Great**, **St Gregory Palamas** and **St Mark of Ephesus**.

Sts Cyril and Methodius and the mission.back: Brothers from **Thessalonica**; mission to **Great Moravia (863)**; Glagolitic alphabet and Slavonic Liturgy. Feast **11 May**.
The first Slavic literary language, made by Cyril and Methodius: **still the liturgical language** of the Russian, Serbian, Bulgarian and other churches.
Cyril's name for the claim that the Liturgy may be served **only in Hebrew, Greek and Latin**.

Sts Cyril and Methodius and the mission.front: Why does the Orthodox Church serve in many languages?
Sts Cyril and Methodius and the mission.back: Following Cyril and Methodius: **the Gospel and the Liturgy are given in the language of the people**.

The filioque: a question of the Creed, a.front: Filioque: the history of the addition
The filioque: a question of the Creed, a.back: Latin, "**and from the Son**": the Western addition to the Creed's "proceeds from the Father". First at **Toledo (589)**; sung in Rome **1014**.

The filioque: a question of the Creed, a.front: What does the Orthodox Church teach about the Spirit and the Son?
The filioque: a question of the Creed, a.back: The Spirit **proceeds from the Father** and is **sent through the Son** in time; with **St Gregory of Cyprus (1285)**, he also **shines forth eternally through the Son**.

1054: the schism as an event and as a pr.back: **Cardinal Humbert** laid a bull excommunicating Patriarch **Michael Keroularios** on the altar of Hagia Sophia; a synod excommunicated the legates.
**Unleavened bread** in the Western Eucharist; a point of dispute in 1053 to 1054. The Orthodox use leavened bread.

1054: the schism as an event and as a pr.front: Why do historians see 1054 as a process rather than one event?
1054: the schism as an event and as a pr.back: The bull named **persons, not churches**; communion lingered in places; the break became complete gradually, made popular by **1204**.

The Crusades and the sack of Constantino.back: The **Fourth Crusade** took and plundered the city; a **Latin Empire** and Latin patriarch until **1261**.
Pope Urban II preached the **First Crusade**, after **Alexios I Komnenos** asked for help.

The Crusades and the sack of Constantino.front: Why did 1204 deepen the division more than 1054?
The Crusades and the sack of Constantino.back: It made the schism **a matter of people and memory**: plunder, Latin hierarchies over Orthodox flocks, an empire broken.

St Gregory Palamas and the hesychast cou.back: Athonite monk, archbishop of **Thessalonica**; *Triads*; defender of the hesychasts. Feast **14 November** and **2nd Sunday of Lent**.
From *hēsychía*, "stillness": the tradition of **inner stillness and unceasing prayer**, aiming at the vision of the **uncreated light**.
Philosopher-monk who held the **light of Tabor created** and God unknowable except by reason; condemned **10 June 1341**.
Constantinople councils that vindicated Palamas; the **Tomos of 1351** affirmed the **essence-energies distinction**.

The councils of union: Lyons (1274), Flo.back: Union decree ***Laetentur caeli*** (6 July 1439), signed by most Greeks but **rejected by the Orthodox Church**; repudiated by a synod in **1484**.
Metropolitan of Ephesus, **the only bishop who refused to sign at Florence**. Feast **19 January**.

The councils of union: Lyons (1274), Flo.front: Why were Lyons and Florence not received, though signed?
The councils of union: Lyons (1274), Flo.back: **Union must be in the faith, not a signature**: clergy, monks and people refused, and the Church's reception decides.

The fall of Constantinople (1453).back: Taken by **Sultan Mehmed II** after a siege from 6 April; **Constantine XI Palaiologos** died fighting; Hagia Sophia made a mosque.
Anti-unionist disciple of Mark of Ephesus; **first patriarch under the Ottomans** (January 1454), head of the **Rum millet**.
The **Ottoman community of all Orthodox Christians**, under the patriarch of Constantinople as civil and spiritual head.

Looking back: the councils of Christ and.front: How does each of the seven councils protect salvation?
Looking back: the councils of Christ and.back: Only God deifies (325); the Spirit is God (381); Mary bore God (431); our whole nature is joined (451); **God suffered** (553); **our will is healed** (681); **God became visible** (787).

Looking back: the councils of Christ and.front: What does the Byzantine history show about who decides the faith?
Looking back: the councils of Christ and.back: **Not emperors and not majorities**: Monothelitism, Iconoclasm, Hieria, Lyons and Florence were all overturned by the Church's reception.

Context: how to read a Father of the Chu.front: Father of the Church (the four marks)
Context: how to read a Father of the Chu.back: **Orthodox doctrine**, **holiness of life**, **antiquity**, and **reception by the Church**.

Context: how to read a Father of the Chu.front: Does the age of the Fathers end, in Orthodox teaching?
Context: how to read a Father of the Chu.back: **No.** The Church is always patristic (Florovsky): Symeon, Palamas and later saints are Fathers too. Western handbooks often stop at **John of Damascus**.

Context: how to read a Father of the Chu.front: Five habits for reading a Father
Context: how to read a Father of the Chu.back: Know **his question**; know **his audience**; read him **with the other Fathers**; read him **in prayer**; **look for Christ**.

St Ignatius of Antioch: the letters of a.back: "**Medicine of immortality**": Ignatius's name for the Eucharist (*Ephesians* 20).

St Ignatius of Antioch: the letters of a.front: "I am the wheat of God" (Ignatius, Romans 4)
St Ignatius of Antioch: the letters of a.back: "...let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that I may be found **the pure bread of Christ**."

St Ignatius of Antioch: the letters of a.front: How does the Church read Ignatius's longing for martyrdom?
St Ignatius of Antioch: the letters of a.back: Not as seeking death, but as **refusing escape by compromise** and desiring **union with Christ**; he was already condemned.

St Irenaeus of Lyons: \"become what we a.front: "Become what we are" (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5, preface)
St Irenaeus of Lyons: \"become what we a.back: Christ "did, through His transcendent love, **become what we are, that He might bring us to be even what He is Himself**": the first great statement of **theosis**.
"**The knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by the obedience of Mary**" (*Against Heresies* 3.22.4).

St Irenaeus of Lyons: \"become what we a.front: How does Irenaeus picture Adam and Eve at creation?
St Irenaeus of Lyons: \"become what we a.back: **Like children**, made to **grow** into God's likeness; the fall interrupted the growth and Christ resumes it.

St Irenaeus: \"the glory of God is a liv.front: "The glory of God is a living man" (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 4.20.7)
St Irenaeus: \"the glory of God is a liv.back: "...and **the life of man consists in beholding God**." Often quoted without its second half.

St Irenaeus: \"the glory of God is a liv.front: Why, for Irenaeus, does God stay invisible even in revelation?
St Irenaeus: \"the glory of God is a liv.back: So that man "should **always possess something towards which he might advance**": endless growth into God.

St Athanasius: On the Incarnation.front: "He was made man that we might be made God"
St Athanasius: On the Incarnation.back: St Athanasius, ***On the Incarnation* 54.3**: the shortest statement of theosis in the Fathers.
"**Corruption**": in Athanasius, the creature's slide back toward the nothing it came from, after turning from God.

St Athanasius: On the Incarnation.front: What is the "divine dilemma" in On the Incarnation?
St Athanasius: On the Incarnation.back: God could neither let his creature perish nor revoke the sentence of death; **repentance could not undo corruption**, so the Word took a body, died for all, and clothed it with **incorruption**.

St Athanasius: On the Incarnation.front: What does Athanasius's image of the ruined portrait teach?
St Athanasius: On the Incarnation.back: The Word, like a painter, **came himself to restore his image** in the same human material (ch. 14).

St Athanasius: the Life of Antony and th.back: Egyptian hermit who gave away all at Matthew 19:21; father of monks. Feast **17 January**. His *Life* by Athanasius, about **357 to 360**.

St Athanasius: the Life of Antony and th.front: How do the Life of Antony and the Orations against the Arians fit together?
St Athanasius: the Life of Antony and th.back: The *Orations* defend **the Son's full Godhead**; the *Life* shows **what it makes possible**: a human being restored by grace.

St Basil the Great: On the Holy Spirit.front: "The honour paid to the image passes on to the prototype"
St Basil the Great: On the Holy Spirit.back: St Basil, ***On the Holy Spirit* 18.45**, of the Son as the Father's image; later applied to **icons** by John of Damascus and Nicaea II.

St Basil the Great: On the Holy Spirit.front: What was the doxology dispute behind On the Holy Spirit?
St Basil the Great: On the Holy Spirit.back: Basil used "Glory to the Father **with** the Son, **together with** the Holy Spirit", attacked as making the Spirit equal; he defended it from Scripture and worship.
Teaching handed down in practice, **with the same force as Scripture**: the sign of the cross, facing east, the epiclesis, triple immersion (*On the Holy Spirit* 27).

St Basil the Great: the Hexaemeron, the.back: "**The six days**": Basil's nine homilies on Genesis 1 (370s): creation good, ordered, from nothing.
Basil's "**new city**" outside Caesarea (about 369 to 372): church, **hospital**, hostel, poorhouse and leper housing.

St Basil the Great: the Hexaemeron, the.front: Liturgy of St Basil (ten times a year)
St Basil the Great: the Hexaemeron, the.back: Sundays of Lent (not Palm Sunday), Holy Thursday, Holy Saturday, eves of **Nativity** and **Theophany**, and **1 January**.

St Gregory the Theologian: the Theologic.back: St Gregory's **Orations 27 to 31**, preached in the **Anastasia** chapel, Constantinople: on God, the Son and the Spirit.
**St John the Evangelist**, **St Gregory of Nazianzus**, **St Symeon the New Theologian**.

St Gregory the Theologian: the Theologic.front: Who may speak about God, according to Oration 27?
St Gregory the Theologian: the Theologic.back: "Not to every one": those **purified in soul and body**, at the right time and **within certain limits**.

St Gregory the Theologian: \"that which.front: "That which He has not assumed He has not healed"
St Gregory the Theologian: \"that which.back: St Gregory, ***Letter 101, to Cledonius*** (about 382), against Apollinarius: Christ must have **a whole human nature**, mind included.

St Gregory the Theologian: \"that which.front: How does Gregory's rule decide the question of Christ's human will?
St Gregory the Theologian: \"that which.back: If Christ took no human will, **our will is not healed**: so the Sixth Council (681) confessed two wills.
The **mind** or spiritual intellect; Apollinarius said the Word replaced Christ's human *noûs*.

St Gregory of Nyssa: the endless ascent.front: Epéktasis in St Gregory of Nyssa
St Gregory of Nyssa: the endless ascent.back: From Philippians 3:13, "**reaching forth**": Gregory of Nyssa's word for the **soul's endless stretching toward God**.

St Gregory of Nyssa: the endless ascent.front: Life of Moses (Gregory of Nyssa, about 390)
St Gregory of Nyssa: the endless ascent.back: The soul's ascent as **light** (the bush), **cloud**, and **darkness** (Sinai): knowing God by unknowing.

St Gregory of Nyssa: the endless ascent.front: Why is perfection never a resting place, for Gregory of Nyssa?
St Gregory of Nyssa: the endless ascent.back: **God is infinite** (*ápeiros*), so the creature can always grow: **each arrival is a new beginning**.

St Ephrem the Syrian: theology as song.back: Deacon of **Nisibis** and **Edessa**, poet in Syriac, "**Harp of the Spirit**". Feast **28 January**.
Syriac **teaching hymn**, sung by choirs: Ephrem's form for teaching doctrine.

St Ephrem the Syrian: theology as song.front: How did St Ephrem oppose the Arians?
St Ephrem the Syrian: theology as song.back: As "**pryers**" who tried to search out the Son's generation: **wonder, not dissection**, is the fit response to God.

St John Chrysostom: the preacher of Anti.back: "**Golden-mouthed**"; priest in Antioch, archbishop of Constantinople **398**; died in exile **14 September 407**. Feast **13 November**.

St John Chrysostom: the preacher of Anti.front: What does Chrysostom teach in Homily 50 on Matthew?
St John Chrysostom: the preacher of Anti.back: "**Wouldest thou do honor to Christ's body? Neglect Him not when naked**": Christ on the altar and Christ in the poor are one.
Synod led by **Theophilus of Alexandria** that deposed Chrysostom; he was recalled, then exiled again in 404.

St John Chrysostom: On the Priesthood an.back: Six books, a dialogue with his friend Basil: **the height and the danger** of the priestly office.

St John Chrysostom: On the Priesthood an.front: Who wrote the anaphora of the Liturgy of St John Chrysostom?
St John Chrysostom: On the Priesthood an.back: Tradition: **Chrysostom**. Scholars (Taft): he **reworked an older Antiochene anaphora** (of the Twelve Apostles). The two views agree he shaped it.
"**Not loving silver**": freedom from greed, praised in Chrysostom's troparion as "non-avariciousness".

Reading: St John Chrysostom's Paschal Ho.back: Sermon under **Chrysostom's** name read at **Paschal Matins**, the people standing: "If any man be devout and loveth God..."

Reading: St John Chrysostom's Paschal Ho.front: Why does the Paschal Homily invite even those who did not fast?
Reading: St John Chrysostom's Paschal Ho.back: Pascha is **God's gift, not a reward for the strong**: like the labourers of Matthew 20, the last receive as the first.

Reading: St John Chrysostom's Paschal Ho.front: What does the Paschal Homily say happened when Hades received Christ?
Reading: St John Chrysostom's Paschal Ho.back: "**It took a body, and met God face to face**": death swallowed God and was destroyed; "not one dead remaineth in the grave".

St Cyril of Alexandria: the one Christ.back: **Communication of properties**: because Christ is one person, what is human is said of God (God died) and what is divine of the man.

St Cyril of Alexandria: the one Christ.front: What is Cyril's central conviction about Christ?
St Cyril of Alexandria: the one Christ.back: **One subject**: everything Christ did and suffered, the **one Word incarnate** did and suffered; "the Word was made flesh".
Christ's flesh is **life-giving because it is the Word's own flesh**: the ground of the Eucharist.

The Dionysian writings: the divine names.back: *Divine Names*, *Mystical Theology*, *Celestial* and *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, ten letters; **about 500** by modern dating; traditionally **St Dionysius the Areopagite** (Acts 17:34).
**Cataphatic**: affirming (God is good). **Apophatic**: denying (God is beyond good). In Dionysius, **the way of denial goes higher**.
The **three stages** of the spiritual life, from Dionysius.

St Maximus the Confessor: the Logos and.back: Each creature's **principle in the divine Word**, God's intention for it; the many *lógoi* are **one Logos**.
**Uncreated/created**, **intelligible/sensible**, **heaven/earth**, **paradise/world**, **male/female**: man was made to unite them; **Christ does**.

St Maximus the Confessor: the Logos and.front: How does St Maximus see the Incarnation's place in creation?
St Maximus the Confessor: the Logos and.back: Not only a remedy for sin: **the purpose of creation from the beginning**, God uniting the world to himself in Christ.

St Maximus the Confessor: love and the p.back: "**Dispassion**": freedom from the passions, not indifference; the step before **love** in Maximus's chain.
"**Self-love**", love of oneself apart from God: **the root of all passions** (Maximus).

St Maximus the Confessor: love and the p.front: What is the chain of virtues in Maximus's Chapters on Love?
St Maximus the Confessor: love and the p.back: **Faith → fear of God → self-control → patience → hope → dispassion → love**.

St John of Damascus: the Exact Expositio.front: The Fount of Knowledge (John of Damascus)
St John of Damascus: the Exact Expositio.back: Three parts: ***Dialectica*** (terms), ***On Heresies***, and the ***Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith*** (100 chapters, 4 books).

St John of Damascus: the Exact Expositio.front: How does the Exact Exposition open its account of God?
St John of Damascus: the Exact Expositio.back: God is "**ineffable and incomprehensible**", yet not left unknown: we receive what **Law, Prophets, Apostles and Evangelists** delivered, "**not removing everlasting boundaries**".

St John of Damascus: on the holy images.front: Why, for John of Damascus, were images rare in the Old Testament?
St John of Damascus: on the holy images.back: **No one can depict the invisible, formless God**; but **after God became man**, what was seen may be shown.

St John of Damascus: on the holy images.front: Why does Salmond's John of Damascus say "worshipping" images?
St John of Damascus: on the holy images.back: Older English for ***proskýnēsis*** (venerating), **not *latreía***, the worship due to God alone.

St Symeon the New Theologian: the experi.front: St Symeon the New Theologian (949 to 1022)
St Symeon the New Theologian: the experi.back: Abbot of **St Mamas**, Constantinople; *Hymns of Divine Love*; exiled 1009. Feast **12 March**.

St Symeon the New Theologian: the experi.front: What is St Symeon's central teaching about grace?
St Symeon the New Theologian: the experi.back: The grace of the Spirit given in baptism is meant to be **consciously experienced**, sought with tears; it is seen as **uncreated light**.
"**The Pious**": monk of Stoudios, **spiritual father** of Symeon the New Theologian.

St Gregory Palamas: essence and energies.back: God's **essence** (*ousía*): unknowable, unshared. His **energies** (*enérgeiai*): **uncreated**, God himself acting, in which we truly share.

St Gregory Palamas: essence and energies.front: Why must the energies be uncreated, for Palamas?
St Gregory Palamas: essence and energies.back: If grace were created, **we would never meet God himself**; theosis would be a created substitute.

St Gregory Palamas: essence and energies.front: How does the essence-energies distinction avoid pantheism?
St Gregory Palamas: essence and energies.back: The **essence** is shared only by Father, Son and Spirit; **the energies** are shared with creatures, who become god **by grace, never by essence**.

St Gregory Palamas: the light of Tabor a.back: The light of the Transfiguration (6 August): for Palamas, **uncreated, the glory of God**, seen by eyes transformed by grace.
"**Navel-souled**": Barlaam's mocking name for the hesychasts and their bodily posture in prayer.

St Gregory Palamas: the light of Tabor a.front: What place does Palamas give the body in prayer?
St Gregory Palamas: the light of Tabor a.back: Bodily stillness **helps gather the scattered mind into the heart**; the body is not evil and **shares in deification**.

Where the Fathers differ: theologoumena,.back: A **theological opinion** of a Father or Fathers, allowed by the Church but not required as dogma (distinction of **Vasily Bolotov**).
St Vincent of Lérins: hold "**that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all**": **universality, antiquity, consent**.

Where the Fathers differ: theologoumena,.front: How do Orthodox writers receive Blessed Augustine?
Where the Fathers differ: theologoumena,.back: Two views: **a Father with errors** (Fr Seraphim Rose); or **a saint to follow with great caution** on grace and the Trinity (Fr John Romanides).

Where the Fathers differ: theologoumena,.front: How do Orthodox writers receive Gregory of Nyssa's hope for the restoration of all?
Where the Fathers differ: theologoumena,.back: Three views: **an error the Church corrected**; **never condemned**, a theologoumenon; or **texts interpolated** (St Germanos).

Looking back: the Fathers in their own w.back: **Christ and theosis** as the subject; **theology from prayer**; **fidelity, not novelty**; **the body matters**; **endless growth** into God.

Looking back: the Fathers in their own w.front: Where should a beginner start reading the Fathers?
Looking back: the Fathers in their own w.back: **Athanasius, *On the Incarnation***; then **Chrysostom's homilies**; then **Gregory's Theological Orations**; then the ***Exact Exposition*** as reference.

Context: the spiritual life as the Creed.back: **Of the Holy Spirit** (*Pneuma*), not 'inward' as opposed to bodily. A spiritual life is one in which the Spirit given in baptism is active.

Context: the spiritual life as the Creed.front: katharsis, phōtismos, theōsis: the three stages
Context: the spiritual life as the Creed.back: **Purification**, **illumination**, **union (deification)**: the Fathers' common outline of the spiritual road, never watertight.
**Co-working** of God's grace and human freedom. God gives everything; a person must still consent and labour.

The aim of the Christian life: acquiring.front: St Seraphim of Sarov (born 1754 or 1759, died 1833)
The aim of the Christian life: acquiring.back: Russian monk, hermit and elder of Sarov; glorified **1903**; feast **2 January**. Greeted all with 'Christ is risen'.

The aim of the Christian life: acquiring.front: What did St Seraphim tell Motovilov (1831) is the aim of the Christian life?
The aim of the Christian life: acquiring.back: **The acquisition of the Holy Spirit of God.** Prayer, fasting, vigil and almsgiving are **means**, fruitful only when done **for Christ's sake**.

The aim of the Christian life: acquiring.front: Why does the Church insist that ascetic practices are means, not ends?
The aim of the Christian life: acquiring.back: A fast or rule kept for pride **misses the point**; progress is measured by fruit (**humility, love, peace**), not by quantity of practice.

What prayer is, and its three kinds.front: What does the Church teach prayer is, first of all?
What prayer is, and its three kinds.back: **Communion with God**: standing before Him with mind and heart. Words help; they are not the substance.

What prayer is, and its three kinds.front: The three settings of Orthodox prayer
What prayer is, and its three kinds.back: **Liturgical** (the services, primary), **the daily rule**, and **inner or unceasing prayer** (above all the Jesus Prayer).
**Attention** in prayer. Wandering is normal; consenting to it is the fault. The cure is to bring the mind back.

The rule of prayer and the icon corner.back: The fixed daily prayer, morning and evening, **set with a confessor** and fitted to a person's life.
The **prayer rope**: knotted wool, often 33, 50 or 100 knots, used to count Jesus Prayers or prostrations.

The rule of prayer and the icon corner.front: Three counsels of the spiritual fathers on the prayer rule
The rule of prayer and the icon corner.back: **Keep it small enough to keep**; **do not drop it for lack of feeling**; **change it only with blessing**.

The Jesus Prayer: its words and its root.front: The Jesus Prayer: the usual full form
The Jesus Prayer: its words and its root.back: **Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.**

The Jesus Prayer: its words and its root.front: The Jesus Prayer's roots in Scripture
The Jesus Prayer: its words and its root.back: The **publican** (Luke 18:13), **blind Bartimaeus** (Luke 18:38), the **Name** above every name (Phil. 2:10; Acts 4:12).
The desert monks' **prayer of one phrase**, repeated through the day; Cassian's verse was 'O God, make speed to save me'.

The Jesus Prayer: its words and its root.front: Why is the Jesus Prayer not a magic formula?
The Jesus Prayer: its words and its root.back: In Scripture **a name is the presence of the person**: it works only as faith and repentance call on **a Person who answers**.

Reading: The Way of a Pilgrim on unceasi.back: Anonymous Russian first-person narrative, **printed at Kazan in 1884**; English translation by **R. M. French (1930)**.

Reading: The Way of a Pilgrim on unceasi.front: What first rule does the Pilgrim's elder give him?
Reading: The Way of a Pilgrim on unceasi.back: Say the Prayer **three thousand times a day**, 'without deliberately increasing or diminishing the number': **obedience** sets the measure.

Reading: The Way of a Pilgrim on unceasi.front: The three levels of the Prayer, in the elder's definition
Reading: The Way of a Pilgrim on unceasi.back: **With the lips, in the spirit, in the heart**: oral, of the mind, and of the heart.

Hesychasm: stillness and the prayer of t.back: **Stillness**: outward quiet, silence of the tongue, and inner stilling of thoughts. A *hesychast* seeks it.
Sitting with bowed head, slowed breath, attention drawn to the heart (Nikephoros, **Gregory of Sinai**). **An aid, not the prayer**; to be used with a guide.

Hesychasm: stillness and the prayer of t.front: What did the councils of 1341, 1347 and 1351 defend in hesychasm?
Hesychasm: stillness and the prayer of t.back: That **the body shares in prayer**, that the light of Tabor is **uncreated**, and that God is known in His **energies**, not His essence.

The nous and the heart.back: **The eye of the soul**: the highest faculty, made for **direct knowledge of God**, not discursive reasoning.
**Discursive reason**: thinking in concepts and steps. Good, but not the organ by which God is known.

The nous and the heart.front: What does hesychast prayer seek for the nous?
The nous and the heart.back: Its **return into the heart**, from which it was scattered by the fall: *the mind in the heart* (Theophan).

Watchfulness: nepsis and the guarding of.back: **Watchfulness, sobriety**: constant attention to the thoughts, so nothing enters the heart unnoticed. The Philokalia's Fathers are the 'neptic' Fathers.

Watchfulness: nepsis and the guarding of.front: Two ways to meet a tempting thought, in the Fathers
Watchfulness: nepsis and the guarding of.back: **Refute it** with Scripture (*antirrhēsis*), or **turn from it at once** and call on Jesus. Many hesychasts prefer the second: arguing keeps it alive.
Step 6 of the Ladder: holding one's death before the eyes, which **sobers the mind** and frees it from avarice and grudges.

How a thought becomes a sin: the stages.back: A **thought**: a suggestion, image or impulse arising in the mind, often bringing a passion with it.

How a thought becomes a sin: the stages.front: Is the first appearance of a bad thought a sin?
How a thought becomes a sin: the stages.back: **No.** Provocation is not in our power; **assent** is where sin begins. Christ Himself was tempted.

The passions and the eight evil thoughts.back: A **distorted movement of the soul**: a natural power (desire, anger) turned from God to something that enslaves.
Desert monk who set out the **eight evil thoughts**; his speculative teaching was later condemned, but his **ascetic teaching passed into the tradition**.

The passions and the eight evil thoughts.front: The eight evil thoughts, in order
The passions and the eight evil thoughts.back: **Gluttony, lust, avarice, dejection, anger, akedia, vainglory, pride.**
**Listlessness, despondency**: the restless boredom that makes prayer hateful. Remedy: **perseverance**, staying with the task.

Self-love: the root of the passions.back: **Self-love** in place of God and neighbour. St Maximus calls it the **mother of the passions**.

Self-love: the root of the passions.front: St Maximus: the three first-born passions of self-love
Self-love: the root of the passions.back: **Gluttony, avarice and vainglory**, matching the three temptations of Christ in the desert.
**Humility**: seeing oneself truly before God, receiving every good as gift. Not low self-esteem.

The virtues: love, discernment and dispa.back: **Discernment**: telling good from evil and the right measure from excess. Cassian: 'the mother of all virtues'.
**Dispassion**: not lack of feeling, but freedom from the rule of the passions, so that desire and anger move rightly.

The virtues: love, discernment and dispa.front: What is the summit of the virtues, in the Ladder and St Paul?
The virtues: love, discernment and dispa.back: **Love** (*agapē*): Step 30 is faith, hope and love, and Climacus calls love God Himself (1 Cor. 13:13; 1 John 4:8).

Fasting: why the Church fasts, and how.back: **Christ fasted**; it **restores the order lost in Eden**; it **loosens the passions**; it is **joined to prayer and almsgiving**.
**Great Lent**; the **Apostles' Fast** (to 29 June); the **Dormition Fast** (1–14 August); the **Nativity Fast** (15 November–24 December).
Abstaining from **meat, dairy, eggs, fish with a backbone**, and often **wine and oil**; applied **by economy** with a confessor.

Almsgiving and the love of the poor.back: **Almsgiving**, from *eleos*, **mercy**: showing others the mercy one asks of God.

Almsgiving and the love of the poor.front: Chrysostom (Homily 50 on Matthew): Christ's body on the altar and in the poor
Almsgiving and the love of the poor.back: **One Christ**: 'Would you do honor to Christ's body? Neglect Him not when naked.'
The **hospital and poorhouse** St Basil the Great built at Caesarea.

Repentance: metanoia, mourning and tears.back: **Change of mind**: the turning of the whole person back to God. Also the name of a bow or prostration.
**Joy-making sorrow**: Climacus's word (Step 7) for godly mourning (*penthos*), full of consolation.

Repentance: metanoia, mourning and tears.front: Remorse, repentance and despair: the difference
Repentance: metanoia, mourning and tears.back: Remorse grieves consequences; **repentance** grieves turning from God and returns; **despair** has lost hope in mercy. Judas regretted; **Peter repented**.

Confession in practice.back: A **penance** given in confession: medicine, not punishment.

Confession in practice.front: Why do Orthodox churches differ on confessing before every Communion?
Confession in practice.back: Russian usage **keeps examination and Communion together**; Greek and Antiochian usage keeps confession **for healing and need**, with frequent Communion. Both are received.
In Greek practice, a priest **specifically blessed by his bishop** to hear confessions.

Spiritual fathers, elders and obedience.back: **Elder** (Greek / Slavonic): a spiritual father of great experience and grace, often a monk.
The **revelation of thoughts** to one's elder: a thought revealed loses its power.

Spiritual fathers, elders and obedience.front: What is the sign of a true elder, as against an abusive one?
Spiritual fathers, elders and obedience.back: **A true elder leads to Christ and to freedom, never to himself**; he does not control, claim infallibility or keep people dependent.

Prelest: spiritual delusion.back: **Spiritual delusion** (Slavonic / Greek): believing oneself advanced or favoured with revelations while deceived by pride, imagination or demons.
**Refuse visions**; **do not imagine in prayer**; **prize repentance**; **reveal everything** to a spiritual father; stay in the Church's life.
Russian bishop, author of *The Arena*; the classic modern teacher on **prelest**.

Spiritual warfare and the unseen enemy.front: What does the Church teach about the demons?
Spiritual warfare and the unseen enemy.back: **Fallen angels**, created good, real and personal but **limited and defeated by Christ**; they act chiefly through **thoughts** and cannot force the will.
St **Nikodemos**'s Greek adaptation of Scupoli's *Spiritual Combat*, further revised in Russian by St **Theophan the Recluse**.

Spiritual warfare and the unseen enemy.front: St Antony's discovery about the demons
Spiritual warfare and the unseen enemy.back: They are **powerless before the cross, the Name of Christ, prayer and humility**; fear of them is their weapon.

The Philokalia: the anthology of the nep.back: 'Love of the beautiful': anthology of the **neptic Fathers**, 4th–15th century, compiled by **Sts Nikodemos the Hagiorite and Makarios of Corinth**.
**St Paisius Velichkovsky**'s Slavonic Philokalia; St Theophan's expanded Russian version followed **from 1877**.
**Twelve volumes**, with commentary, by Fr Dumitru Stăniloae.

The Ladder of Divine Ascent: St John of.back: Abbot of **Sinai**, author of *The Ladder*; commemorated **30 March** and on the **Fourth Sunday of Great Lent**.

The Ladder of Divine Ascent: St John of.front: Why does the Ladder have thirty steps?
The Ladder of Divine Ascent: St John of.back: After **the thirty years of Christ's hidden life** before His baptism; the image is **Jacob's ladder** (Gen. 28:12).

The Ladder of Divine Ascent: St John of.front: The Ladder's steps in five groups
The Ladder of Divine Ascent: St John of.back: **1–3** break with the world; **4–7** foundations; **8–23** passions; **24–26** meekness, humility, discernment; **27–30** stillness, prayer, dispassion, love.

Monasticism: its beginnings and its form.back: **Father of monks**; gave away his inheritance about 270 and withdrew into the Egyptian desert. Life by **St Athanasius**.
Founder of the **coenobitic** (common-life) monastery in Upper Egypt.

Monasticism: its beginnings and its form.front: The three forms of monastic life
Monasticism: its beginnings and its form.back: **Eremitic** (hermit, Antony), **coenobitic** (community, Pachomius), and **skete or lavra** (small groups round an elder).

Monastic vows and the monastic day.back: The monastic degrees: **robe-wearer**, **small schema** (full vows, new name), **great schema** (highest).
**Obedience, chastity and poverty** (non-possessiveness, *aktēmosynē*), with perseverance until death.
The **abbot** of a monastery (abbess: *hēgoumenē*), its spiritual father or mother.

Mount Athos: the Holy Mountain.back: First great coenobitic monastery on Athos, founded by **St Athanasios the Athonite** with Emperor Nikephoros Phokas.

Mount Athos: the Holy Mountain.front: The twenty ruling monasteries of Athos

Mount Athos: the Holy Mountain.back: **Self-governing** within Greece through the **Holy Community at Karyes**; **spiritually under the Ecumenical Patriarchate**.

The Russian elders: Paisius Velichkovsky.back: Monk of Athos and **Neamț** (Moldavia); translated the Philokalia into **Slavonic**; source of the Russian and Romanian revival of eldership.
Monastery near Kozelsk, **the centre of 19th-century Russian eldership**: Sts Leonid, Macarius, Ambrose, Nektary. Closed 1923, returned 1987.
The most famous Optina elder; founded **Shamordino** convent; glorified **1988**.

The spiritual life in the world: family,.back: **No.** The Gospel and the goal belong to every baptised person; married life is **its own ascetic way**.
Chrysostom's **'little church'**: the household with its icon corner, prayers and blessings.

The spiritual life in the world: family,.front: What do the marriage crowns signify, spiritually?
The spiritual life in the world: family,.back: **Royal crowns and martyrs' crowns**: each spouse **dies to self-will** for the other.

Looking back: one road from baptism to t.front: Five sentences that sum up the Orthodox spiritual life
Looking back: one road from baptism to t.back: It is **the Spirit's life in the Church**; **assent, not provocation, is sin**; passions heal slowly, **forgiveness is immediate**; **walk with a guide**; the sign of progress is **humility and love**.

Looking back: one road from baptism to t.front: How Stage 10 relates to the doctrine of theosis
Looking back: one road from baptism to t.back: It is **the practical road** to the union with God taught in Stage 3, through purification, illumination and union.

Context: one Church in many lands after.back: '**Self-headed**': a church that **elects its own primate** and is fully self-governing.
**Self-governing**, but its primate is **confirmed by a mother church** (e.g. Finland, Sinai, Japan).

Context: one Church in many lands after.front: The fourteen autocephalous churches in Constantinople's diptychs
Context: one Church in many lands after.back: **Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, Russia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Georgia, Cyprus, Greece, Poland, Albania, Czech Lands and Slovakia.**

The Patriarchate under the Ottomans: the.front: Rum millet: the Patriarch as ethnarch
The Patriarchate under the Ottomans: the.back: The Ottoman '**Roman nation**': all Orthodox subjects, under the Ecumenical Patriarch as **ethnarch**, civil as well as spiritual head.
Scholar-monk installed by **Mehmed II in January 1454**, the first patriarch under Ottoman rule; opponent of the Union of Florence.
District of Istanbul where the **Ecumenical Patriarchate** has been seated, at St George's, **since 1601**.

The neomartyrs of the Ottoman centuries.back: A **new martyr**: a Christian killed for the faith under Ottoman (Islamic) rule, often for refusing or renouncing conversion.
Athonite monk who preached through Greece and Albania, founding some **200 schools**; executed **1779**; feast **24 August**.
St **Nikodemos the Hagiorite**'s collection of the **lives and services of the neomartyrs**, published in Venice.

The Orthodox confessions of the seventee.front: The Orthodox Confession of Peter Mogila (Iași, 1642)
The Orthodox confessions of the seventee.back: Catechism by **St Peter Mogila**, Metropolitan of Kiev, approved at the **Synod of Iași (1642)** and by the Eastern patriarchs (1643).
Approved the **Confession of Dositheos**, answering point by point the Calvinist confession attributed to **Cyril Lucaris**.

The Orthodox confessions of the seventee.front: How do Orthodox theologians weigh the 17th-century confessions?
The Orthodox confessions of the seventee.back: Some treat them as **symbolic books** second only to the councils; others (Florovsky, Meyendorff) as **local, of their time, with Latin terms**, to be read by the Fathers. Both: their content is Orthodox.

The Kollyvades and the patristic revival.back: **Boiled wheat** blessed at memorials for the departed; it gave the Kollyvades their (originally mocking) name.
Memorials on **Saturday, not Sunday**; **frequent Communion**; **publishing the Fathers**; keeping the **Typikon and canons**.
Athonite editor of the **Philokalia** (1782), the **Pedalion** (1800), the Neon Martyrologion and *Unseen Warfare*; glorified **1955**.

Reading: the Encyclical of the Eastern P.back: Letter of the patriarchs of **Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem** and their synods, in reply to Pius IX, on how the faith is kept.
